units.la: I. Nter Sathanæ μυεγοτέχνα stratagemata & artificia, quibus hominum saluti insidiatur, haud postremum illud est, quod iis persuadere laborat, ut vel salutis causas veras & falsas commiscendo, salute excidant: vel salutis ejusdem causas & media separando, vel saltem non eo, quo par est, pretio eas æstimando, vel studio & fervore conveniente prosequendo, ejusdem naufragium patiantur. Neque vel olim caruit, vel hodieque caret contentio isthæc tristi successu, ut nunquam defuerint in Ecclesia, nec hodieque desint, qui vel ἀμιxτὰ μιγνύειν, lucem cum tenebris; Paganismum & Judaismum cum Christianismo; Philosophiam, verbi Divini luce non collustratam, cum religione; justitiam veram cum falsa, alienam cum propria commiscere satagant, uti veterum Nazaræorum, Judaizantium, Pelagianorum, & recentiorum Papistarum & Socinianorum præcipua dogmata fidem faciunt: vel indivulso nexu cohærentia, velut Dei & rerum Divinarum notitiam & praxin atque zelum Dei, scientiam & conscientiam, fidem & charitatem, ejusque opera, distrahere & separare, quasi vel illa absque hac, vel hæc absque illa præsidii satis ad salutem haberet, religioni non ducant. uti oppositæ hæreses veterum, Gnosticorum inprimis & Gnosimachorum, nec non recentiorum, Libertinorum, Antinomorum, Fanaticorum, Catabaptistarum, Pontificiorum quinetiam & Socinianorum eorundem, iisque supparasitantium Remonstrantium, aliorumque etiam, κυείας circa religionem δόξαν comprobant.
units.tr: Among Satan's [μυεγοτέχνα] stratagems and devices, by which he lays snares for men's salvation, this is no small one: he labours to persuade them either to mix the true and false causes of salvation together and so fall away from salvation; or to separate the causes and means of salvation from one another; or at least not to value them at their proper worth, or not to pursue them with due zeal and fervour, and so suffer shipwreck of it. This contest has never lacked, and still lacks, a sad outcome. There have never been wanting in the Church, and there are not wanting now, those who strive to mix [ἀμικτὰ μιγνύειν] what cannot be mixed: light with darkness; paganism and Judaism with Christianity; philosophy, not illumined by the light of the divine Word, with religion; true righteousness with false, and another's righteousness with one's own. The principal doctrines of the ancient Nazarenes, the Judaizers, the Pelagians, and of the more recent Papists and Socinians bear this out. Others do not hesitate to divide and separate what cohere in an indissoluble bond: the knowledge of God and divine things from practice, and zeal for God; knowledge from conscience; faith from love and its works, as if either could suffice for salvation without the other. So the opposing heresies of the ancients, above all the Gnostics and the Gnosimachi, and of more recent times, the Libertines, Antinomians, Fanatics, Catabaptists, and also the Papists and the Socinians themselves, together with the Remonstrants who hang on them as parasites, and others besides, prove their [κυείας] vanity [δόξαν] in matters of religion.

units.la: II. De posterioribus illis differendi paucis occasionem, imo & necessitatem imponit grassans in ipsa Ecclesiæ Dei viscera Sathanæ, antiqui Serpentis, πανουργία illa, qua ipsos Dei filios aggressus, aliorum quidem animos pestifera hac opinione imbuere conatur, quòd in rerum Divinarum qualicunque scientia & cognitione acquiescentes, certam salutis spem habeant, licet in eorum, quæ ex verbo Dei cognoverunt, praxi languescant, vel deficiant penitus: alios verò errore opposito ita dementat,ut transmissa rerum Divinarum cognitione, exactiore illa cum primis, omnem consequendæ salutis æternæ spem, ejúsque proram & puppim in vitæ sanctimonia,& exercitiis inprimis pietatis externis,repositam habeant. Quorum in contrarium currentium errori ejusmodi remedium adhibere conabimur,ut ostensuri simus,tum utrosque illos quadam ἀμστεἰα ἡ ἀνϑολωῆς, veterum & recentiorum hæreticorum,Gnosticorum inprimis,vel Gnosimachorum, eorúmque vestigiis insistentium aliorum,castris implicari: tum quod palmarium est, à Regio tramite veritatis, quæ voluntatis Divinæ cognitionem cum obedientia adamantino nexu sic copulat,ut nec Dei cognitionem probet,quæ insita quadam vi ad obedientiam non inclinat & ducit; nec veram obedientiam æstimet, quæ ex veri Dei cognitione,ceu fonte quodam irriguo pietatis, non derivatur, in transversum abripi. Quæ duo ad compescendam, & intra gyrum atque limite sententiæ mediæ, quam semper Ecclesia Christi ex Dei verbo professa est, coercendam dissidentium quorum vis aberrationem, magnum inprimis pondus habebunt.
units.tr: II. The rampant error of Satan, the old Serpent, in the very bowels of the Church of God, obliges and even necessitates that I say a few words about the latter. He attacks the very sons of God with that cunning [πανουργία]; some he tries to imbue with the pestilent opinion that, resting content with some knowledge of divine things, however slight, they have a sure hope of salvation even though they grow lax or utterly fail in the practice of what they have learned from the Word of God. Others he drives mad with the opposite error, so that, having set aside the knowledge of divine things, above all the more exact knowledge, they place all their hope of obtaining eternal salvation, and its prow and stern, in holiness of life and especially in outward exercises of piety. To the error of these opposing parties we shall try to apply a remedy of this kind, so that we may show, first, that both groups are entangled in the camp of a certain [ἀμστεἰα ἡ ἀνϑολωῆς] error of the ancient and recent heretics, above all the Gnosticorum and the Gnosimachorum, and of others who tread in their footsteps. Second, and this is the chief point, that they are dragged off the royal road of truth, which so binds the knowledge of God's will to obedience with an adamantine bond that it neither approves a knowledge of God which, lacking some inner force, does not incline and lead to obedience, nor esteems a true obedience which is not derived from the true knowledge of God, as from a living spring of piety. These two points will carry great weight in restraining the dissenters, and in keeping them within the circle and boundary of the middle opinion which the Church of Christ has always professed from the Word of God.

units.la: Etenim verissimè Solomon dixit: Quod extitit, idem est, quod existet; & quod factum est, id est, quod fiet, ואין כל חדש תחת השמש & non est novum quicquam sub Sole, Eccl.I.9. Id quoque hac in re accidit, ubi veteres in Ecclesia hæretici & errones novis facem veluti errorum prætulerunt; prioribus illis Gnostici, qui cognitionis suæ typho inflati, alia omnia susque deque habuerunt, & alto supercilio despexerunt: posterioribus Gnosimachi, qui scientiæ & cognitionis Divinæ jurati hostes, vitam innocenter & piè transactam salutis æternæ causam unicam statuerunt. De utrisque,& quas illi in Ecclesia partes fecerint,& sequentium temporum decursu reliquerint,ante omnia certiora quædam eruere conabimur, ut quas partes devii à veritate sectentur, constet.
units.tr: Indeed Solomon most truly said: What has been is what will be, and what has been done is what will be done, [ואין כל חדש תחת השמש] and there is nothing new under the sun, Eccl. 1.9. This has also happened in this matter, when the ancient heretics and errorists in the Church held up new torches, as it were, of errors. The former were the Gnostici, who, puffed up with the conceit of their knowledge, held everything else of no account and looked down upon it with haughty disdain. The latter were the Gnosimachi, sworn enemies of knowledge and of divine understanding, who made an innocent and pious life the sole cause of eternal salvation. Before all else we shall try to bring out certain facts about both, and about the parts they played in the Church and left behind in the course of the following ages, so that it may be clear which parts those who stray from the truth follow.

units.la: IV. GNOSTICIS à γνώσει cognitione nomen est,ob eximiam perfectámqne rerum Divinarum scientiam, quam sibi vendicabant. Eorum authorem veteres Simonem Magum perhibent, quem à S. Paulo perstringi ajunt,sic Timotheum exhortatnre: O Timothee, depositum custodi, vitans profanas inanitates vocum, & ἀντιϑέσεις ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως oppositiones falsò nominatæ cognitionis,quam quidam spondentes circa fidem naufragium passi sunt, 1.Tim.VI.20.21. In præterito loquitur de certis hominibus, qui falsam illam scientiam magnificis promissis jactan- Utrique ... habuerunt. jactantes, fide exciderint. Eos vero Simonem Magum Samaritanum, ejusque sectatores, qui variis nominibus insigniti sunt, fuisse, & Irenæus lib.1.20. & Theodoretus ad h.1.Tom.III. p.490. persuadent. Et Theodoretus quidem eos, qui à Simone processerunt, Gnosticos appellatos ait, quia ἃ σεσήγηκε ἡ θεία γραφὴ, ταῦτα ὁ Θεὸς αὐτοῖς ἀπεκάλυψε, quæ Divina Scriptura tacuit, Deus sibi revelaverit. Quæ ipsa tamen πάσης δυσσεβείας καὶ ἀσελγείας πλένα esse omni impietate & lascivia testatur. A qua impietate Borboritarum, quasi Cænosorum, λομεν iis hæsit. Nam & Epiphanius Hæref.21. & post eum Nicetas Choniates Thes. Orth. Fid. Lib.IV.1. prodiderunt, Simonem Magum impurissimam mystagogiam suam γνώσεως cognitionis nomine venditasse. A Simone Mago per Menandrum, Basilidem, Nicolaum, Corpocratem, Valentinum, quos Gnosticorum satores Epiphanius hær.27. facit, γνώσης illa disseminata est ad eos usque hæreticos, qui, dissimulatis progenitoribus suis, ab eximia rerum Divinarum intelligentia nomen Gnosticorum sibi arrogarunt. Quod Epiphanius idem Aniceti tempore, altero post Christum seculo, factum tradidit. Illi ergo, qui S. Pauli tempore γνῶσιν cognitionem singularem, & abstrusarum rerum, sibi vendicarent, Simon Magus, αἱρέσεως ἀρχηγὸς haresεos dux, uti Eusebius Hist. Eccl. lib.1.13. appellat, & sectatores ejus, pestiferas propagines, Gnosticorum nomen paulo post sibi imponentes, Lucina velut obstetricante, protruserunt. Quos etiam Epistolam S. Pauli priorem, quòd in ea se vivis coloribus notatos, & stigmate veluti compunctos agnoscerent, repudiasse, Clemens Alexandrinus Strom.lib.1. author est.
units.tr: IV. The Gnostici take their name from γνῶσις, knowledge, on account of the outstanding and perfect understanding of divine things which they claimed for themselves. The ancients say that Simon Magus was their author, whom they say Paul rebuked when he exhorted Timothy: O Timothy, guard what has been entrusted to you, avoiding the profane empty talk and the oppositions of falsely named knowledge [ἀντιθέσεις ψευδωνύμου γνώσεως], which some, professing it, have made shipwreck of in the faith, 1 Tim. 6.20–21. He speaks of certain men in the past who, boasting of a false knowledge with grand promises, fell away from the faith. That these men were Simon Magus the Samaritan and his followers, who were given various names, both Irenaeus lib.1.20. and Theodoret ad h.1. Tom.III. p.490. assert. Theodoret indeed says that those who came from Simon were called Gnostics because what the divine Scripture has kept silent, God has revealed to them, [ἃ σεσήγηκε ἡ θεία γραφὴ, ταῦτα ὁ Θεὸς αὐτοῖς ἀπεκάλυψε]. Yet he testifies that this knowledge was full of all impiety and lewdness [πάσης δυσσεβείας καὶ ἀσελγείας πλένα]. From this impiety they were called Borborites, that is, Mire-men [λομεν]. For both Epiphanius Hær.21. and, after him, Nicetas Choniates Thes. Orth. Fid. Lib.IV.1. relate that Simon Magus sold his most impure mystagogy under the name of knowledge [γνώσεως]. From Simon Magus, through Menander, Basilides, Nicolaus, Carpocrates and Valentinus, whom Epiphanius hær.27. makes the fathers of the Gnostics, this knowledge [γνώσης] was spread abroad, down to those heretics who, concealing their forefathers, claimed for themselves the name of Gnostics from their outstanding grasp of divine things. Epiphanius records that this happened in the time of Anicetus, in the second century after Christ. Those, therefore, who in the time of Paul claimed a singular knowledge [γνῶσιν] of hidden things were Simon Magus, the leader of the heresy [αἱρέσεως ἀρχηγὸς], as Eusebius Hist. Eccl. lib.1.13. calls him, and his followers, who soon afterwards took the name of Gnostics and brought forth their pestilent offspring, with Lucina, as it were, assisting at the birth. Clement of Alexandria Strom. lib.1. reports that they rejected the earlier Epistle of Paul because they recognised themselves portrayed in it in lively colours, and pricked as though by a brand.

units.la: V. Præterea iidem γνώσεως jactatæ authores feriri à S.Paulo eodem videntur, sic scribentes: De idolythis novimus, quòd omnes cognitionem habeamus. Γνῶσις δὲ Cognitio autem inflat, charitas vero, ædificat, 1. Cor.VIII.1. Nam & Gnosticos sine omni pudore, solo cognitionis obtentu, ad mensas dæmoniorum accessisse, & idolothyta comedisse, Irenæus adv.hær.lib.1.cap.1. & Tryphon apud Justinum Martyrem prodidit. Eosdem Christum pro re nata abnegasse, & a nulla spurcitie abstinuisse, veteres testantur. Licet enim Desiderius Heraldus Not.ad Minut. pag.76. & post ipsum Doctiss. Christianus Kortholtius Diatr. II. de Calumn. in veteres Christ.p.65. pleraque, quæ Gnosticis spurcissima, velut incestus, cædes intantum, cæsorum viscerationes, aliáque nefanda, veteres affricuerunt, falsa, & odio sectæ ab hominibus perversè religiosis, qui Dei opus mendaciis proveh posse existimarent, confícta esse, perte iderunt; quin & credulitatem Epiphanii, levibus auditiunculis fidem habentis, Casaubonus Exerc. ad Baron. XV. sect. 7. traduxerit; suspecta tamen ea in re Epiphanii authoritas esse non debet, quia non tantum libros Gnosticorum à se lectos, sed etiam viros fide dignos, & insuper impuritatum talium patratores, in quos incidens, & per aetatem lubricam ab earum foeminis ad societatem scelerum invitatus, oretenus facinora sua narrantium, αὐτοπτῶς haec audiverit, citat. ut tot seculorum fidem temere solicitandam non videri, merito Doctiss. Thomasio in praestantissimo Schediasmate Historico pag. 34. videatur.
units.tr: V. Moreover, the same boasters of knowledge seem to be struck by Paul in the same place, when he writes: We know that we all have knowledge about idol-meats. Knowledge [Γνῶσις δὲ] puffs up, but love builds up, 1 Cor. 8.1. For Irenaeus adv. hær. lib.1. cap.1. and Trypho, as reported by Justin Martyr, relate that the Gnostics, without any shame, under the mere pretext of knowledge, came to the tables of demons and ate idol-meats. The ancients testify that the same men, when occasion arose, denied Christ, and abstained from no filthiness. For although Desiderius Heraldus Not. ad Minut. pag.76. and, after him, the most learned Christian Kortholt Diatr. II. de Calumn. in veteres Christ. p.65. have shown that many of the most foul things which the ancients attributed to the Gnostics, such as incest, murders, the mutilation of the slain, and other unspeakable deeds, were invented, and false, and fabricated out of hatred for the sect by men perversely religious, who thought they could advance the work of God by lies, yet Casaubon Exerc. ad Baron. XV. sect. 7. has censured the credulity of Epiphanius, who gave credit to slight hearsay. Nevertheless, the authority of Epiphanius ought not to be regarded as suspect in this matter, because he cites not only the books of the Gnostics which he had read, but also trustworthy men, and besides, perpetrators of such impurities whom he met with and, as a youth prone to slip, was invited by their women into fellowship in crimes; and he heard these things autopsy [αὐτοπτῶς] from those recounting their own deeds. Thus the faith of so many centuries ought not to be lightly disturbed, as the most learned Thomasius shows in his excellent Historical Schediasma pag. 34.

units.la: VI. Cum Cognitionis suae perfectae opinione & nefariae spurcitiae generibus Indifferentismum & ἀναμαρτησίαν Impeccantiam Gnostici conjunxerunt. Irenaeus enim de Carpocrate & sociis, qui in Gnosticorum censu fuerunt, sic lib.I.24. loquitur: Vitam quidem luxuriosam, sententiam autem impiam ad velamen malitiae ipsorum nomine abutuntur. Quorum judicium justum est, recepturos dignam suis operibus retributionem. Et in tantum insania effraenati sunt, uti & omnia, quaecunque sunt irreligiosa & impia, potestatem habere operandi se dicant. Sola enim humana opinione negotia mala & bona dicunt. Neque licitas duntaxat, sed etiam justas foeditates suas dixerunt, afferentes, hac ratione mundanis Principibus, hoc est, malis geniis debitum quasi suum exsolvendum esse. Negarunt igitur, se, foedissima quaeque patrantes, ullius peccati vel corruptionis alligari, vel alligari & pollui ullo modo posse. Christianos vero orthodoxos, quos pudore peccandi mente vel sermone tangi cernebant, velut idiotas, imperitos, imo & ψυχικὰς Psychicos, seu animales falsè riserunt, & ab iis aeque atque à χοικοῖς terrestribus, tertio hominum genere, Christiana religione carentium se distinguentes, sibi πνευματικῶν Spiritualium, & τελείων Perfectorum nomen arrogarunt, dictitantes, imperfectioribus opera bona necessaria esse, ut ad locum mediocrem enitantur, sibi perfectis & spiritualibus neutiquam illa necessaria esse; eò denique provecti vaesaniae, ut fidei & operibus suam illam magnificam γνῶσιν maximo cum supercilio anteponerent. Plurima eam in rem Irenaeus de Haer. lib.1. cap.1. dixit, ubi inter alia, ex mente Valentinianorum, qui Gnosticorum genus fuerunt; ὡς γὰρ τὸ χοϊκὸν ἀδύνατον σωτηρίας μεταχεῖν, οὕτως πάλιν τὸ πνευματικὸν (ὁ θέλεσιν αὐτοὶ εἶναι) ἀδύνατον φθορᾶν καθέξαθαι, καὶ οὐ ὁπρίως συγκαταχωρώντων πεφέξεσιν. οὐ γὰρ τέρπον ζευγὸς ὁ βορβόρῳ καταπεθεὶς οὐκ ἀποβάλλει πὼ κάλλονην αὑτὸ, ἀλλὰ πὼ ἰδίαν φύσιν ἀφυλάττει, ξ βορβόρφ μηδὲν ἀδικήσου τὸν χρυσόν. "Οὕτω δὲ καὶ αὐτὰς λέγεσι, καὶ οὐ ὁπρίως ὁπολίαν ὁλικῶς προέξεσι καὶ ἀγένωντος, μηδὲν αὐτὰς ἀξιοβλάπτεσθαι, μηδὲ ἀπο-βάλλειν τῶ πνευματικὴν ὑπόστασιν. Sicut Choicum, terrestre, nullo modo salutis particeps esse posse dicunt, ita spirituale, (quod ipsi se esse volunt) ea conditione esse, ut nullo prorsus modo interitum atque corruptionem recipere queat, quibuscunque in flagitiis sceleribusque tandem versetur. Sicut enim aurum in cœno positum pulchritudinem suam haud proinde amittit, verùm naturam suam incolumen servat, nec detrimenti quicquam ei a cœno afferri potest: eodem modo sese quoque, uibuslibet tandem in materialibus actionibus versantur, nihil hinc ladi, nec spiritualis jacturam facere. Quo etiam fit, ut eorum persectissimi quique, omnia ea, quae legis interdicto prohibentur, & de quibus affirmat Scriptura, quod qui haec faciunt, Regni Dei haereditatem minimè consequentur, (ἀδέως) sine ullo metu perpetrant. Nam & ea, quae idolis immolata sunt, libere ac sine ullo discrimine comedunt, neque iis se inquinari arbitrantur. Cujus insani furoris refutatione opus non est, quia, uti scite Irenæus idem lib. I. cap. ult. loquitur, adversus eos victoria est sententia eorum manifestatio. Nihilominus Gnosticorum hanc haeresin postea sub Gratiano Imperatore A.CCCLXXXI. in Hispaniis Priscillianus, ejúsque asseclae Priscillianista amplexi sunt. de quibus prolixè ejusdem aetatis scriptor, Sulpitius Severus, Bituricensis Episcopus, in fine lib. II. Hist. scripsit. Quos etiam verbum scientia & perfectionis sibi vendicasse, Hieronymus Epist. ad Clesiph. testis est.
units.tr: VI. The Gnostics joined indifferentism and impeccability [ἀναμαρτησία] to their conviction of perfect knowledge and to kinds of foul filthiness. Irenaeus speaks thus of Carpocrates and his companions, who were counted among the Gnostics, in book 1, chapter 24: They abuse a luxurious life and an impious doctrine under the cover of their own name for wickedness. Their judgement is just: they will receive a reward fitting their works. And they are so unbridled in their madness that they claim the power to do all things whatever that are irreligious and impious. For they say that deeds are bad or good only by human opinion. They called not only their lusts lawful but even just, asserting that by this method they paid what they owed, as it were their own due, to the worldly princes, that is, to the evil spirits. They therefore denied that they, committing the most shameful acts, were bound by any sin or corruption, or could in any way be bound or polluted. But the orthodox Christians, whom they saw touched by shame at sinning in mind or word, they falsely mocked as simple, unlearned, and even psychic [ψυχικὰς], or animal men. Distinguishing themselves from these, and equally from the earthly [χοϊκοῖς] men, a third class of people lacking the Christian religion, they claimed for themselves the names spiritual [πνευματικῶν] and perfect [τελείων]. They insisted that good works were necessary for the less perfect, so that these might strive toward a middling place, but were in no way necessary for themselves, who were perfect and spiritual. At last they advanced to such madness that they placed their magnificent knowledge [γνῶσιν] above faith and works with the greatest arrogance. Irenaeus says a great deal on this point in Against Heresies, book 1, chapter 1, where, among other things, he writes, according to the mind of the Valentinians, who were a kind of Gnostic: "For just as the earthly cannot partake of salvation, so again the spiritual (which they themselves wish to be) cannot possibly be subject to corruption, whatever they associate with. For a gold ring thrown into mire does not lose its beauty but keeps its own nature, and the mire can do no harm to the gold." [ὡς γὰρ τὸ χοϊκὸν ἀδύνατον σωτηρίας μετέχειν, οὕτως πάλιν τὸ πνευματικὸν ἀδύνατον φθορᾶς καθέξασθαι, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως συγκαταχρώμενον ἀπολέσαι. οὐ γὰρ τὸ ἐν βορβόρῳ καταπεσὸν χρυσίον ἀποβάλλει τὴν καλλονὴν αὐτοῦ, ἀλλὰ τὴν ἰδίαν φύσιν φυλάττει, τοῦ βορβόρου μηδὲν αὐτῷ δυναμένου βλάψαι.] "And they say thus: just as gold cast into mire does not lose its beauty but keeps its own nature, so the spiritual man, however he may be involved in filth, is in no way harmed and does not lose his spiritual substance." [Οὕτω δὲ καὶ αὐτοὶ λέγουσι, καὶ οὐδὲν ὅλως ἀποβάλλειν τὸ πνευματικὸν ὑπόστασιν, μηδὲν αὐτὸ ἀξιοβλαπτεῖσθαι.] They say that the earthly, being such, can in no way share in salvation; so the spiritual (which they wish themselves to be), on the condition that it cannot in any way receive destruction or corruption, whatever wicked crimes it may at last commit. For just as gold lying in mud does not thereby lose its beauty but keeps its nature intact, and no harm can come to it from the mud, so they too, whatever material actions they engage in, are harmed by nothing and suffer no loss of the spiritual. From this it also follows that the most perfect among them commit, without any fear [ἀδεῶς], all those things that the prohibition of the Law forbids, and of which Scripture affirms that those who do them will by no means obtain the inheritance of the kingdom of God. For they eat freely and without any distinction the things sacrificed to idols, and do not think themselves defiled by them. There is no need to refute this insane madness, since, as Irenaeus wisely says in the same book, chapter last, their own declaration is their victory over them. Nevertheless, under the Emperor Gratian in the year 381, Priscillian and his followers in Spain embraced this heresy of the Gnostics, the Priscillianists. Sulpicius Severus, the writer of the same age and bishop of Bourges, wrote at length about them at the end of book 2 of his History. Jerome, in his letter to Clesiphon, bears witness that they also claimed for themselves the word "knowledge" and "perfection".

units.la: VII.
units.tr: VII.

units.la: Attamen profligatissimae haereseos radicem fodere juvabit. Simon Magus, Samaritanus, ejus author, fidem Christianam cum Philosophorum placitis & insaniente sapientia commiscere instituerat. Testes enim Irenæus, Epiphanius, alii sunt, eum, & sectatores ejus, una cum Jesu imagine Platonis quoque, Pythagorae & Aristotelis imagines coluisse. Cùmque Philosophiae paganae fundamentum fuerit capitalis error de duobus contrariis rerum principiis aeternis; Simon, è Principis Magorum Zoroastris, Schola, Magus & ipse, duos Deos ἀντιέχνας sibi adversantes, bonum & malum, adoptavit; illum Veteris, hunc Novi Testamenti praesidem constituens. Malo Deo, quem ἀεὶ πρὸς δύναμιν sinistram potentiam vocabant, tum impietate quavis, tum magicis artibus inprimis, Gnostici litarunt. Nam Gnosticos aequè atque Simonem magiae deditos fuisse, veteres testantur. Quos inter sic Irenæus lib. I. 20. scribit: Horum mystici Sacerdotes libidinosè quidem vivunt, Magias autem perficiunt, quemadmodum potest unusquisque ipsorum. Exorcismis enim & incantationibus utuntur. Amatoria quoque & agogima, & qui dicuntur paredri, & oniropompi, & quacun-que
units.tr: Yet it will be worth our while to dig up the root of this most abandoned heresy. Simon Magus, the Samaritan, its author, had undertaken to mix the Christian faith with the doctrines of the philosophers and with a frenzied wisdom. Irenaeus, Epiphanius and others bear witness that he and his followers worshipped, together with the image of Jesus, also the images of Plato, Pythagoras and Aristotle. And since the chief error of pagan philosophy was the doctrine of two contrary eternal principles of things, Simon, himself a magus, who came from the school of Zoroaster, the chief of the Magi, adopted two gods opposed to each other, good and evil, setting the one over the Old Testament and the other over the New. The Gnostics sacrificed to the evil god, whom they called the left-hand power [ἀεὶ πρὸς δύναμιν], by every kind of impiety and above all by magical arts. For the ancients testify that the Gnostics, like Simon himself, were devoted to magic. Among them Irenaeus writes thus in book 1, chapter 20: "Their mystic priests live lustfully, and they practise magic, each of them as he is able. For they use exorcisms and incantations, love charms and attractions, and those called paredri and oniropompi, and whatever other trifles [parerga] are diligently practised among them."

units.la: Eorum au-thor Simon Magus, haeresin illam à Magis, Zoroastre inprimis, & Philoso-phia musa-tus est. que sunt alia parerga ( legendum perierga ) apud eos studiosè exercentur. Fuerunt ergo Gnoslici iisdem artibus dediti, quibus & γνώσεω, qua voce LXX. Interpretes vocem Hebraeam בְּיִדְעֹנִי quæ sciolos, magos, divinatores, seu abstrusissima quæque ex astris & aliunde divinantes & docentes, significat, reddunt.
units.tr: Their author Simon Magus was inspired with this heresy by the Magi, above all by Zoroaster, and was instructed in philosophy. The Gnostics were therefore devoted to the same arts as those by which the Seventy render the Hebrew word [בְּיִדְעֹנִי] by the word "gnoseis" [γνώσεις], which means conjurers, magicians, diviners, or those who divine and teach the most hidden things from the stars and other sources.

units.la: VIII.
units.tr: VIII.

units.la: Philosophi porro, Pythagoras inprimis, Plato & Aristoteles, Philosophiæ eam partem, quæ de rebus æternis & maximè honorabilibus, hoc est, Divinis, agit, γνῶσιν τῶν ὄντων notitiam entium. Plato γνῶσιν τῶν ἀληθῶς καὶ ὄντως ὄντων notitiam entium, quæ verè & reapse talia sunt; Aristoteles γνῶσιν τῶν ὄντων, ἡ ὂν ᾗ ὂν, notitiam entium quatenus entia sunt, definiunt. In hac ergo notitia summam sapientiæ ita illi collocarunt, ut eam vel ab actione circa illa entia plane separaverint, vel saltem supra actionem multis parasangis extulerint. Nam Aristoteles ad Nicomach. lib. X. 7. felicitatem absolutam definit ἐνέργειαν κατ' ἀρετὴν actionem secundum virtutem optimum optimæ facultatis. Optimam verò facultatem facit νοῦν intelligentiam, eò quod τὴν Φύσιν ἄρχειν δοκεῖ καὶ ἡγεῖσθαι, καὶ ἔννοιαν ἔχειν περὶ καλῶν καὶ θείων, secundum naturam videatur, dominari ac præesse, & habere notitiam de præclaris & Divinis, sive θεῖον Divinum quid sit ipsum, sive eorum, quæ in nobis sunt, θειώτατον Divinissimum. Unde τελείων εὐδαιμονίαν perfectam felicitatem in θεωρητικῇ, facultate contemplandi, consistere, conficit. Addit tamen, ad facultatem illam contemplandi solos eos pertingere, quorum animum virtus moralis priùs ἀπὸ τῆς ὑλικῆς ἀλογίας τῶν παθῶν ab affectuum face rationi contraria purgaverit. Quasi videlicet id vel sine vera sapientia & θεογνωσίᾳ cont ngere possit: vel sapientia vera fit, quæ ad amorem rei cognitæ, adeòque virtutem recta non dirigit: vel non contemplatio Dei sine actione vel inclinatione ad agendum mera impietas & profanitas sit.
units.tr: Moreover, the philosophers, above all Pythagoras, Plato and Aristotle, treated that part of philosophy which deals with eternal and especially honourable things, that is, divine things, as "knowledge of beings" [γνῶσιν τῶν ὄντων]. Plato defined it as "knowledge of beings that are truly and really such" [γνῶσιν τῶν ἀληθῶς καὶ ὄντως ὄντων], that is, of beings which are what they are in truth and in fact. Aristotle defined it as "knowledge of beings, insofar as they are beings" [γνῶσιν τῶν ὄντων, ἡ ὂν ᾗ ὂν]. In this knowledge they placed the highest wisdom in such a way that they either separated it completely from action concerning those beings, or at least raised it far above action by many parasangs. For Aristotle, ad Nicomach. lib. X. 7., defines absolute happiness as "activity according to virtue, the best activity of the best faculty" [ἐνέργειαν κατ' ἀρετὴν]. He makes the best faculty the intellect [νοῦν], because it seems to rule and lead nature, and to have understanding of noble and divine things, that is, to dominate and preside over what is in accordance with nature, and to have knowledge of the excellent and divine, whether of what the divine itself is [θεῖον], or of what is most divine [θειώτατον] among the things in us. Hence he concludes that perfect happiness [τελείων εὐδαιμονίαν] consists in the contemplative faculty [θεωρητικῇ]. He adds, however, that only those reach that faculty whose soul moral virtue has first purged of the irrational [ἀπὸ τῆς ὑλικῆς ἀλογίας τῶν παθῶν], that is, of the passions, the torch of affections contrary to reason. As if, forsooth, this could be attained without true wisdom and knowledge of God; or as if that were true wisdom which does not direct a person to love of the thing known, and so to right virtue; or as if contemplation of God without action, or without an inclination to act, were not sheer impiety and profanity.

units.la: IX. Potissima Aristotelis, contemplativam vitam, ceu persectæ beatitudinis consortem, commendantis, ratio inde petita est, quòd Dei ipsius vita & felicitas in cognitione, seu contemplatione consistat. Sic enim ad Nicom. lib. X. 8. argutatur: Perfectam beatitudinem contemplandi quandam actionem esse, vel inde constare posse, quòd Deos putamus beatos & felices esse. Quales autem actiones iis adscribere oportet? An justas? Num ridiculi viderentur, si exercerent commercia, & deposita reddèrent, atque alia hujusmodi facerent? An fortes? quòd suslineant formidolosa, subeántque pericula, quia honestum sit? An liberales? Cui verò dabunt? Absurdum verò, si ipsis etiam sit nummus, aut aliquid tale. Si verò temtemperantes, quidnam essent? An importuna laus fuerit, quòd pravas cupiditates non habeant? Percurrentibus denique nobis per omnia videbuntur, τὰ ἀξὲι τὰς πράξεις , quæ ad actiones pertinent, μικρὰ καὶ Θεῶν ἀνάξια parva & Dîis indigna. Sed tamen vivere omnes existimant ipsos, proin etiam agere. Non enim profecto dormiunt, ut Eudymio. Viventi ergo actione detracta, & praterea magis effectione, τί λείπεταγ πλὴν Θεωρίας quid restat praeter contemplationem? ὥστε ἡ ἐ Θεὸς ἐνέργεια μακαριότης ἀφθαρτος Θεωρητικὴ ἂν εἴη. Quare Dei actio felicitate antecellens beatissima erit. Et ex humanis igitur, quæ huic maxime cognata est, beatissima erit. Rationem hanc ex Epicuro, nisi fallor, mutuatus est. Nam & is Dei beatitudinem in otiosa sui contemplatione collocavit. Cæterum hæc delira & impia ratio est, quæ & hominis beatitudinem ex Dei beatitudine metitur, & Deum omni virtute, atque actione virtutis insanè spoliat. Atqui ὁ Θεὸς ἀγάπη Deus charitas est. 1. Joh. IV. 8. Neque in tota illa incomprehensibili essentia & vita Dei quicquam ita noscibile est, ut charitas ejus. Hac enim movente hominem ad sui imaginem condidit, & eundem per peccatum abalienatum servat. Ipse Salvator τελειότητα perfectionem Dei non obscure ostendit in ejus amore, quo is & inimicos suos dilexit, & Solem bonis ac malis, pluviam justis & injustis impartitur, Matth. V. 44. 45. &c. coll. cum Rom. V. 10. Neque quicquam justitiæ & misericordiæ Divinæ temperamento decantatius est. At nec puerilius quicquam dici poterat, quàm quòd sine commerciis & depositis nulla justitia; sine formidolosis nulla fortitudo; sine pecuniis nulla liberalitas; sine pravis cupiditatibus nulla temperantia locum habere vel exerceri possit. Sapientius longè Plato in Theæteto: Θεὸς ἐδαμὴ ἐδαμῶς ἀδικεῖ, ἀλλ' ὡς ὅιόν τε δικαιότατος. καὶ οὐκ ἔστιν αὐτῷ ὁμοιώτερον ἐδὲν, ἢ ὃς ἂν ἡμῶν γένηται δικαιότατος. Deus nullo uspiam modo injustus est, sed plane justissimus. Nec ei similius inveniri potest quicquam, quàm qui justissimus est.
units.tr: IX. The chief reason that Aristotle takes up, commending the contemplative life as the partner of perfect blessedness, is that the life and happiness of God himself consist in knowing, or contemplation. For in the same book, ad Nicom. lib. X. 8., he argues thus: that perfect blessedness is a kind of contemplative activity may be seen from this, that we think the gods are blessed and happy. But what actions must we attribute to them? Just ones? Would they not seem ridiculous if they engaged in trade, returned deposits and did other things of that sort? Brave ones? Would they endure frightening things and undergo dangers, because that is honourable? Generous ones? To whom would they give? It would be absurd if they even had money, or anything of the kind. And if they were temperate, what would they be? Would it not be an inappropriate praise, that they have no base desires? In short, if we run through everything, they will seem to have actions which pertain to actions, small and unworthy of the gods [τὰ ἀξὲι τὰς πράξεις, μικρὰ καὶ Θεῶν ἀνάξια]. But still all think they live, and therefore also act. For surely they do not sleep, like Endymion. So when living and acting are taken away, and especially making, what is left but contemplation? So the activity of God, surpassing all others in blessedness, will be the most blessed contemplative activity. Therefore the action of God, excelling in happiness, will be most blessed. And so among human things, that which is most akin to it will be most blessed. I think he borrowed this argument from Epicurus. For Epicurus too placed God's blessedness in an idle contemplation of himself. Yet this is a foolish and impious argument, which measures the blessedness of man by the blessedness of God, and strips God madly of all virtue and of virtuous action. And yet "God is love" [ὁ Θεὸς ἀγάπη]. Deus charitas est. 1 John 4:8. Nor is anything in that whole incomprehensible essence and life of God so knowable as his love. For moved by this he made man in his own image, and he preserves him, though estranged by sin. The Saviour himself plainly shows the perfectionem of God in his love, by which he loved even his enemies, and imparts his sun to the good and evil, and his rain to the just and unjust, Matt. 5:44–45, etc., compared with Rom. 5:10. Nor is anything more often sung of than the temperament of divine justice and mercy. Yet nothing more childish could be said than that there can be no justice without business dealings and deposits; no courage without frightening things; no generosity without money; no temperance without base desires. Far wiser is Plato in the Theaetetus: "God is by no means unjust in any way, but as far as possible most just; and nothing is more like him than whoever among us becomes most just." God is in no way unjust, but altogether most just; nor can anything be found more like him than the one who is most just.

units.la: X. Sed de hoc quicquid sit, abunde constat, Philosophos suos Simonem Magum, & assectlas ejus, Gnosticos eum in errorem induxisse, ut γνῶσιν cognitionem rerum Divinarum ab actione prorsus divellerent, & ex eadem, abdicata pietate omni, sibi summam beatitudinem promitterent.
units.tr: X. But whatever may be the case with this, it is abundantly clear that Simon Magus and his followers, the Gnostics, led their philosophers into error, so that they utterly divorced knowledge of divine things from action, and, having renounced all piety, promised themselves from it the highest blessedness.

units.la: Sed erat tamen illa ψευδώνυμος γνώσις cognitio falsò cognominata. 1. Tim. VI. 20. Proin Christiani veteres, abdicata illa, veram sibi γνῶσιν asseruerunt, sed conjunctam illam cum vera fide, quæ actionis expers non est. Retinuerunt vocabulum γνώσεως etiam Semichristiani Platonici; veluti Pseudo-Mercurius, qui
units.tr: But that was nonetheless a "falsely named knowledge" [ψευδώνυμος γνώσις], knowledge wrongly so called (1 Tim. 6:20). Therefore the early Christians, rejecting that, claimed for themselves a true knowledge [γνῶσιν], but joined to true faith, which is not without action. The semi-Christian Platonists also retained the word "knowledge" [γνώσεως], such as the Pseudo-Mercurius, who

units.la: Græcam è Platone haustam doctrinam Christianæ è libris sacris petitæ miscuit- quam in rem plura Casaubonus Exerc.I.ad Baron.§.10. dixit; duos inprimis ex Pœmandro Mercurii illius Trismegisti locos, in quibus mentio est ῆ γνώσεως, proferens. Mox etiam Clemens Alexandrinus Strom.lib.I. II. III. Didymus Alexandrinus, Evagrius Ponticus,aliíque Gnosticorum nomen, quasi injustis possessoribus ereptum,ita veris Christianis vindicarunt, ut tamen amore nimio Philosophiæ Platonis & Pythagoræ capti,errorem non plane exuerint. Distinguebant enim sicut γνῶσιν eximiam & perfectam ab inchoata & imperfecta; ita etiam Gnosticum à Christianis imperfectioribus seu neophytis, & πνευματικὸν (spirituale), unicè deditum contemplationi, à σαρκικῷ carnali, vitæ activæ vacante. Et illum quidem ἀποδῆ, & tantùm non ἀναμαρτησίαν fecerunt; nutantes ita in alterum extremum, dum incautis loquendi formulis, quales studium ἀνθρωπῆς parere solet, religionem ab obscœnarum libidinum gurgite in contraria propriæ perfectæ cognitionis, ἀναμαρτησίας, sanctitatis,imò & Enthusiasmi juga deduxerunt.
units.tr: mixed Greek doctrine drawn from Plato with Christian doctrine taken from the sacred books. On this point Casaubon, in Exerc. I. ad Baron. §10., has said a good deal, citing above all two passages from the Poimandres of that Mercurius Trismegistus, in which there is mention of ἡ γνώσεως [the knowledge]. Soon afterwards also Clement of Alexandria, Strom. lib. I, II, III., Didymus of Alexandria, Evagrius Ponticus, and others claimed the name Gnosticorum [of the Gnostics], as if snatched from unjust possessors, for true Christians, yet so captivated by excessive love of the philosophy of Plato and Pythagoras that they did not wholly shake off the error. For they distinguished γνῶσιν [knowledge] that is distinguished and perfect from that which is inchoate and imperfect; and in the same way they distinguished the Gnosticum [Gnostic] from the more imperfect Christians or neophytes, and the πνευματικὸν [spiritual] man, devoted solely to contemplation, from the σαρκικῷ [carnal] man, who was given over to the active life. And they indeed made the former ἀποδῆ [without need] and virtually ἀναμαρτησίαν [sinless]; swaying thus to the other extreme, while through careless forms of speech, such as the zeal of ἀνθρωπῆς [human] people is wont to produce, they led religion from the whirlpool of obscene lusts into the opposite yokes of their own perfect knowledge, ἀναμαρτησίας [sinlessness], sanctity, and indeed even Enthusiasm.

units.la: XI.
units.tr: XI.

units.la: Atque consilium isthoc infelix, Philosophiam cum religione Christiana ferruminans, in nervum erupit, emergentibus seculo quarto Messalianus & Pelagianus. Illos enim Enthusiastas appellant veteres, & ipsi sibi nomen Spiritualium imposuerunt: hi ex homine Deum fecerunt: utrique Gnosticorum, non veterum illorum, sed recentiorum,quos contrariam in faciem Clemens Alexandrinus, Evagrius,horúmque similes alii novi Gnostici,gravi censura dignissimi, & eadem ab Hieronymo Epist. ad Ctefiph. merito notati, reformare conati sunt: utrique à Monachis, eximiam præ cæteris cognitionem & sanctitatem affectantibus, oriundi, hominem in hoc seculo sine peccato, &,quod perinde ipsis fuit,sine affectu vivere posse, defenderunt.
units.tr: This unhappy plan, which welded philosophy to the Christian religion, burst forth into a sinew of the faith when the Messalians and Pelagians emerged in the fourth century. The ancients called them Enthusiasts, and they themselves took the name Spirituals. The former made God out of man. Both were offshoots of the Gnostics: not of the ancient Gnostics, but of the more recent ones, whom Clement of Alexandria, Evagrius and other similar new Gnostics, most deserving of severe censure and rightly marked by Jerome in Epist. ad Ctesiphontem, tried to reform by opposing them. Both arose from monks who aspired to a knowledge and holiness surpassing all others, and both maintained that man can live in this world without sin and, what for them amounted to the same thing, without passion.

units.la: XII.
units.tr: XII.

units.la: Afflavit deinceps etiam Gnostica hæc impietas Muhammedem, magnum impostorem illum, qui versutiæ politicæ,qua mundum, ignorantiæ nebulis immersum, subegit; enthusiasmos etiam commiscuit. Nam ab Angelo suo parastata, Gabriele, se ad creatorem usque suum noctu perductum, ingentem lucem, sic præstringentem mentis suæ aciem, ut extra se esset, vidisse, atque ita legem suam, & arcana Divina singularia, dona inprimis & πλσονεκτήματα sua quinque illa celebrata, velut quòd Deus se primam & principem creaturam in cœlo & terra fecerit: quòd in die judicii honoratior omnibus futurus sit: quòd generalis mundi redemptor futurus sit: quod linguarum omnium peritiam habiturus sit : quod denique in prælio victor semper extiturus, & opima spolia reportaturus sit; percepisse mentitus est ; tanto cum successu, ut enthusiasmo illo suo brevi rudem & illiteratum populum sub jugum suum miserit, eique persuaserit, quod maximus omnium Prophetarum,& verè Divinus sit. Quin & Enthusiasmos suos & dementiam fanaticam,perinde ut olim Gnostici, per effrœnem lusum & festivitatem, ambitionem, & libidinem insatiabilem, raptus Poeticos, furores Martios, aliáque ejusmodi gnaviter executus est; atque hæc inter, stupendum cogitatu & dictu! fundamenta imperii illius jecit, quod totus mundus etiamnum attonitus admiratur. Denique Muhammed palam se Dei Apostolum & Prophetam mentitus, Gnosticos, & cum iisdem Montanum & Manichæum, ejusdem patris Diaboli filios,qui & ipsi se Dei nuntios & Apostolos jactarunt, & veris Christi Apostolis se anteposuerunt, imitatus est.
units.tr: Later this Gnostic impiety also breathed upon Muhammad, that great impostor who, by political cunning, subdued a world sunk in clouds of ignorance, and he mixed enthusiasms into it as well. For he claimed that his angel, Gabriel, his attendant, had led him by night right up to his Creator, and that he had seen a great light which so dazzled the edge of his mind that he was beside himself. Thence, he falsely claimed, he received his law, his singular divine secrets, and especially his gifts and privileges, the famous five: that God made him the first and chief creature in heaven and on earth; that he would be the most honoured of all on the day of judgment; that he would be the general redeemer of the world; that he would have knowledge of all languages; and that finally he would always emerge victorious in battle and carry off the rich spoils. He had such success that by this enthusiasm of his he soon brought a rude and unlettered people under his yoke, and persuaded them that he was the greatest of all prophets and truly divine. Moreover, just as the Gnostics once did, he carried out his enthusiasms and fanatical madness vigorously through unbridled play and revelry, ambition, insatiable lust, poetic raptures, martial frenzies and other things of the kind. Amid these, a thing astonishing to think and say, he laid the foundations of that empire, which the whole world still admires in amazement. Finally, Muhammad openly falsely claimed to be the Apostle and Prophet of God, and in this he imitated the Gnostics, and with them Montanus and Manichaeus, sons of the same father the Devil, who also boasted that they were messengers and apostles of God and set themselves above the true apostles of Christ.

units.la: XIII. Demum in Ecclesiam Theologia gemina, Mystica & Theologia Scholastica incessit; illa Platonicæ, hæc Aristotelicæ Philosophiæ; utraque Gnosticorum,illa recentiorum, hæc vetustiorum tradux. Illa enim sanctimonia quadam & enthusiasmis voluntatem peccatis; hæc penitiore rerum Divinarum notitia & subtilitate curiosa intellectum inscitia exuere contendens,incautos in amorem sui rapuit. Illius antesignanus Pseudo-Dionysius Areopagita, Clemente Alexandrino posterior, fuit. Et,qui eandem primus à Græcis ad Latinos traduxit, Johannes Scotus Erigena, nec non, qui primus artis formam ei imposuit, Hugo de S. Victore, tribus viis, seu virtutibus, purgativa, illuminativa & unitiva eam constare tradiderunt. Quam methodum novissimi etiam scriptores Mystici,Hoburgius,Philippus à S.Trinitate, alii sectantur. nisi quod ultimam viam proprie spectare ad mysticum, imò esse ipsam Theologiam mysticam,Sandæus Theol.Myst. p.360. notavit. Olim quidem Platonici quatuor virtutum gradus constituerunt, asserentes,alias esse Politicas, quæ ex bestia hominem faciunt per μετεχοπάθειαν : alias καθαρτικὰς purgatorias, quæ ex homine dæmonem bonum faciant per ἀπάθειαν: alias illuminativas,seu intellectuales, ex dæmone bono Deum facientes, alias exemplares, seu θεουργικὰς Deificas, ex Deo Patrem Deorum cudentes. Quæ maximam partem ex animæ humanæ non creatione Divina, sed effluxu ex Dei essentia; unde etiam Gnostici animas derivarunt,fluxerunt. Per hos igitur quatuor virtutum gradus animam à comple- Gnosticorum genere originem habet. xu corporis & materiae, quae principium illis omnis malignitatis erat, abjunctam ad Divinam essentiam reduci, atque ita non tantùm similem Deo fieri, sed etiam æqualem, adeóque plane Θεοποιηθῆναι Deificari posse, Porphyrius & Platonici alii statuerunt. Qui virtutum quatuor gradus Platonici ita Christianis mysticis placuerunt, ut refecto primo, quippe ad homines imperfectos, quos Clemens Alexandrinus ψυχικὰς animales appellavit, non ad πνευματικὰς spirituales, & contemplativos, quos solos Theologia mystica informat, attinente, reliquos retinuerint. nisi quòd pro exemplaribus, seu θεωρητικοῖς unitivas, unioni cum Deo, imò & transformationi in ipsum inservientes, dicere maluerunt. Quibus etiam in gradibus haud difficile est Gnosticum reperire. Nam Varinus in Lexico πρακτικὸν, γνωστικὸν & θεωρητικὸν distinguens, per πρακτικὸν eum, qui in via purgativa; γνωστικὸν, qui in illuminativa, & θεωρητικὸν, qui illuminatus jam in unitiva, Deo per contemplationem essentiae ejus uniente, consistit, intelligit. Idem γνῶσιν τὴν Ἀρχὴν ἐκ πνεύματος χάριτος ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις τῶν ἀξίων γινομένην ἐλλαμψιν splendorem, qui per gratiam spiritus in cordibus dignorum fit; definit; loquens de γνώσει quadam eximia, qualem Gnostico suo Clemens, illuminato & unito Theologi Mystici, & perfecto Messaliani asseruerunt. Carolus quoque Herfentius Appar. ad Dion. Areop. Theolog. Myst. p. 3. Theologiam illam Mysticam, quatenus viam unitivam insistit, definivit cognitionem Dei per essentiam seu substantiam; seu etiam Dei, uti in se ipso est, experimentum: vel perfectam & exquisitam Dei cognitionem, super omnem aut sensus aut mentis operationem, supra affirmationem aut negationem, quae intima essentia animae cum essentia Dei unione & conjunctione, cum summa pace, silentio & ignoratione perficitur. Quam definitionem summam esse eorum, quae Dionysius, & ante eum, Platonici de γνώσει cognitione Dei docuerunt, idem asserit.
units.tr: XIII. At last two theologies crept into the Church: the Mystical theology and the Scholastic theology. The former belongs to Platonic philosophy, the latter to Aristotelian. Each is a conduit of Gnosticism: the former of the more recent, the latter of the more ancient. The former, by a certain sanctimony and enthusiasms, strives to strip the will of sins; the latter, by a more searching knowledge of divine things and curious subtlety, strives to strip the intellect of ignorance; and both have carried the unwary away into love of self. Its standard-bearer was Pseudo-Dionysius the Areopagite, who came after Clement of Alexandria. And John Scotus Erigena, who first translated it from the Greeks into Latin, and Hugh of St Victor, who first gave it the form of an art, handed down that it consists of three ways, or virtues: purgative, illuminative and unitive. Later mystical writers, Hoburg and Philip of the Holy Trinity, and others follow this method, except that Sandaeus noted in Theol. Myst. p. 360 that the final way properly looks to the mystical, indeed is itself mystical theology. Of old, indeed, the Platonists set up four grades of virtue, holding that there are some political virtues, which make a man out of a beast through metriopatheia [μετριοπάθεια, moderation of the passions]; others purgative [καθαρτικαί], which make a good demon out of a man through apatheia [ἀπάθεια, freedom from passion]; others illuminative, or intellectual, making God out of a good demon; and others exemplary, or theurgic [θεουργικαί], that is, deifying, forging the Father of the gods out of God. These grades, for the most part, derive from the human soul not by divine creation but by emanation from the essence of God, whence also the Gnostics derived souls. By these four grades of virtue, Porphyry and other Platonists held that the soul, freed from the body and from matter, which for them was the source of all evil, is led back to the divine essence, and thus can become not only like God but even equal to him, and so can plainly be deified [Θεοποιηθῆναι]. The Platonists' four grades pleased Christian mystics so much that, having reworked the first, which pertains to imperfect men whom Clement of Alexandria called animal [ψυχικοί], not to the spiritual [πνευματικοί] and contemplative men alone whom mystical theology informs, they kept the rest; except that for the exemplary grades, or contemplative [θεωρητικοί], they preferred to say unitive, serving union with God and even transformation into him. In these grades it is not difficult to find the Gnostic. For Varinus, in his Lexicon, distinguishing practical [πρακτικόν], gnostic [γνωστικόν] and theoretical [θεωρητικόν], understands by the practical one who is in the purgative way; by the gnostic, one in the illuminative way; and by the theoretical, one who, already illuminated, abides in the unitive way, uniting with God through contemplation of his essence. The same man defines knowledge [γνῶσις] as the illumination [ἐλλαμψις] arising in the hearts of the worthy from the grace of the Spirit, a splendour [ἡ ἀρχὴν ἐκ πνεύματος χάριτος ἐν ταῖς καρδίαις τῶν ἀξίων γινομένην ἐλλαμψιν]; speaking of a certain eminent knowledge, such as Clement claimed for his Gnostic, the illuminated and united one of the mystical theologians, and the perfect one of the Messalians. Charles Herfentius too, in Appar. ad Dion. Areop. Theolog. Myst. p. 3, defined that mystical theology, insofar as it insists on the unitive way, as the knowledge of God through essence or substance, or also the experience of God as he is in himself; or the perfect and exquisite knowledge of God, above every operation of sense or mind, above affirmation or negation, which is accomplished through the union and conjunction of the inmost essence of the soul with the essence of God, with supreme peace, silence and unknowing. He asserts that this definition is the sum of what Dionysius, and before him the Platonists, taught about the knowledge [γνῶσις] of God.

units.la: XIV. De Theologia Scholastica, Gnosticorum partu, dicere ni- hil attinet.
units.tr: XIV. Concerning Scholastic Theology, the Offspring of the Gnostics: There Is No Need to Say More.

units.la: Constat enim satis, illam in contemplatione rerum sublimium, abstrusarum, non revelatarum, feré consumi, & in mera γνώσει, subtilitate, speculationibus argutis & aridis consistere. Cujus etiam authores perfectionem hominis in contemplatione collocantes, actionem infra ejus dignitatem subsidere multùm, definiunt, ea in re Aristoteli suo, qui ut Gnosticorum, ita etiam Scholasticorum parens est, & contemplationem longè actioni praetulit, masculè suffragantes. Quibus jam olim Nicolaus Clemanges, Magister Parisiensis fis, & Archidiaconus Bajacensis, Epist.de Theol.Stud. applicavit illa Pauli: Languent circa quaestiones & pugnas. Quorum etiam infinita volumina,& ineptas quaestiones id in Divino cultu esse posse, quod canis in balneo, Alciatus, celebris ille JCtus, oratione de Legibus Avinione habita, pronuntiavit. Quam in rem plura alibi diximus.
units.tr: It is quite plain that this theology is largely taken up with the contemplation of lofty, abstruse and unrevealed things, and consists of pure gnosis [γνῶσις], subtlety, keen and dry speculations. Its authors place the perfection of man in contemplation and define action as falling far below its dignity. In this they stoutly support their Aristotle, who is the parent of the Gnostics and of the Scholastics alike, and who placed contemplation far above action. Long ago Nicolaus Clemanges, Master of Paris and Archdeacon of Bayeux, applied to them in his Epistle on the Study of Theology those words of Paul: languishing about questions and strifes. Alciatus, that famous jurist, in his oration On the Laws delivered at Avignon, declared that their endless volumes and inept questions could be in divine worship what a dog is in a bath: endless volumes and inept questions could have a place in the worship of God, as a dog has in a bath. We have said more on this matter elsewhere.

units.la: XV. Non ovum ovo similius est, quàm Gnosticorum, tum priorum, tum posteriorum Theologia talis recentiorum, post Reformationis Ecclesiae tempora Ecclesiam infestantium Libertinorum, Enthusiastarum & Mysticorum Theologiae similis est. verè ut mutatis personis eandem scenam agitari constet. Gnostici enim redivivi inprimis Libertini sunt; à Spiritus Libertate, quam sectantur, ita dicti. Capitalia eorum dogmata sunt, existere Deum, qui peccati author sit, adeóque malum Deum: Spiritum hominis ex essentia Dei decerptum, ad ejusdem essentiam redire: Unicum enim esse spiritum, & animarum nostrarum loco Spiritum Dei vivere in nobis, vegetare corpora, nos sustinere, omnésque actiones vitales edere: Quaecunque homo agit, opus Dei esse, & Deum eorum causam formalem esse: Nec bonum, nec malum quicquam esse sua natura, sed sola opinione, judicio, imaginatione bonum vel malum patrantis: Regenerationem hominis in eo consistere, quòd peccatum pro nihilo ducit, & ab opinatione liber est: Placere Deo, quicquid cogitant, dicunt, faciunt: Adulteria, homicidia, incestus non esse peccata, cùm patrantur à regenitis, cognitionem hanc habentibus, quòd nihil natura sua malum sit, sed sola opinione hominis: Regenitos omnes esse in statu Angelico, impeccabiles, & commixtione carnali promiscua sanctificari, liberósque omnis peccati exsortes gignere: Eosdem per regenerationem Deificari, & essentiali Dei justitia justificari: Omnia homini sine exceptione licere; eúmque obligatione omni erga Deum & homines solutum esse: Libertatem hominis consistere in Indifferentia, qua liber agit, quicquid libet: Unicuique appetitum esse pro regula sua, & cor hominis, quocunque eum impulerit, vocationis magistrum illi esse: Omnem omnium in mundo hominum vivendi rationem probari posse: Nemini fas esse, quamcunque ob causam tristari, lamentari, vel quocunque modo affici: Crucem & martyrium rem omnium stultissimam esse.
units.tr: XV. One egg is no more like another than the theology of the Gnostics, both the older and the later kind, is like the theology of the Libertines, Enthusiasts and Mystics who have troubled the Church since the time of the Reformation. It is clear that the same play is being acted, with only the actors changed. For the Gnostics brought back to life are above all the Libertines, so called from the liberty of the Spirit which they pursue. Their chief dogmas are these: that God exists and is the author of sin, and so an evil God; that the spirit of man is torn from the essence of God and returns to that essence; that there is only one spirit, and that in place of our souls the Spirit of God lives in us, quickens our bodies, sustains us and produces all our vital actions; that whatever man does is the work of God, and that God is its formal cause; that nothing is good or evil by its nature, but only by the opinion, judgment or imagination of the one who does it; that the regeneration of man consists in regarding sin as nothing and being free from scruple; that whatever they think, say or do pleases God; that adulteries, murders and incest are not sins when committed by the regenerate, who have this knowledge that nothing is evil by its nature but only by man's opinion; that all the regenerate are in an angelic state, impeccable, and are sanctified by promiscuous carnal intercourse, and beget children free from all sin; that the same persons are deified through regeneration and justified by the essential justice of God; that everything is lawful for man without exception, and that he is released from every obligation towards God and men; that the liberty of man consists in indifference, by which he does whatever he pleases; that each person's appetite is his own rule, and the heart of man, wherever it drives him, is his teacher of vocation; that the way of life of every man in the world can be approved; that it is wrong for anyone to grieve, lament or be affected in any way for any cause; and that the cross and martyrdom are the most foolish things of all.

units.la: XVI. Haec, aliáque assertionum ejusmodi blasphemarum portenta, Calvinus, in Instructione contra Libertinos, & epistola adversus Franciscanum quendam, sectae illius defensorem ad fideles Rhotomagenses, alii que post ipsum notarunt, graviterque refutarunt, in Gnofticorum vetustiorum,& Platonicorum nil non γνώσει cognitioni, judicio & opinioni suæ,ceu unicæ & indeclinabili veri & falsi,boni & mali dijudicandi regulæ, tribuentium, solámque conscientiam & timorem peccati pro peccato venditantium; Indiffrentismum, quinetiam impeccantiam, ἀπαθείας, & Spiritus humani Deificationem propugnantium, impia & horribili officina cusa & excusa sunt. Ita enim Simon Magus, Gnosticorum parens, Irenæo lib.1.20. teste, permisit suis agere,qua vellent, quia secundum gratiam ejus salventur homines,non secundum operas justas. Nec enim esse naturaliter operas justas, sed ex accidentia. Idem c.24. de Carpocrate & sociis, Gnosticorum sectæ innexis: Sola, inquit, humana opinione negotia mala & bona dicunt. Quæcunque religiosa & impia sunt, potestatem habere operandi se dicunt. Quæ cuncta ita comparata sunt, ut per ea ἕτερον Εὐαγγέλιον aliud Evangelium, Gal.1: 6. alium Christum prædicari, opera & doctrinam Diaboli Christo & Evangelio ejus surrogari, & gratiam Dei in lasciviam carnis commutari, facilè appareat.
units.tr: XVI. These and other monstrous blasphemous assertions of this kind were noted by Calvin, in his Instruction against the Libertines and in his letter to the faithful of Rouen against a certain Franciscan, a defender of that sect, and were seriously refuted by others after him. They were forged and re-forged in the impious and horrible workshop of the older Gnostics and of the Platonists, who attributed everything to gnosis [γνῶσει] and to their own knowledge, judgment and opinion, as the one unchangeable rule for distinguishing true from false and good from evil; who put forward conscience and the fear of sin alone as sin; and who defended indifferentism, even impeccability, apatheia [ἀπαθείας], and the deification of the human spirit. For Simon Magus, the parent of the Gnostics, as Irenaeus testifies (lib. 1, c. 20), allowed his followers to do whatever they wished, because men are saved according to his grace and not according to just works. For just works are not natural, but accidental. Irenaeus says the same of Carpocrates and his associates, who belong to the Gnostic sect (c. 24): They say, he says, that deeds are evil and good only by human opinion. Whatever is religious and impious, they say they have the power to do. All these things are so arranged that through them, as is easily seen, another Gospel [ἕτερον Εὐαγγέλιον] (Gal. 1:6) is preached, another Christ is put in place of Christ, the works and teaching of the Devil are substituted for Christ and his Gospel, and the grace of God is turned into licence of the flesh.

units.la: XVII. Affines Gnosticis & Libertinis sunt Spirituum fortium nomine infames, qui & Deistæ in Gallia appellantur, non eo sensu, quo Prateolus Elench. hæref. lib.IV. Antitrinitarios & Arianos Deistas dixit,sed κατ' ἀνλιφεσιν, quia Deum optimè se cognoscere professi, ejus providentiam, revelationem & gratiam, & quicquid homini carnali displicet, eadémque ratione Deum ipsum haud obscurè abnegant.quomodo olim à gentibus deviẽtis Imperatores belli Africani, Germanici &c. dicti sunt. Solius nempe γνώστως suæ typho inflati illi, ferociunt, & ambulantes לב בשררות in firmitudine cordis sui, avertentes illud à Jehova Deo suo,Deut XXIX.18.19. spiritus sui nequissimi fortitudinem crepare audent. Quo hominum ἀπηλγικοτων genere nihil nequius est, dum & Deum se retinere profitentur, & quæ Dei sunt, impuro ore abnegantes, Christianæ simplicitati impiè illudunt. Qui & Degrues appellari se amant,quia non,ut cæteri grues ad mysteria religionis Christianæ contremiscunt,sed alto supercilio illa despiciunt, & Sardonio risu prosequuntur. Quorum utinam non tristissima seges agrum Domini suffocasset,& quotidie suffocaret! XVIII. Gnosticorum posteriorum illorum, Messalianorum, & illorum, quos ab obscœnarum libidinum profundo ad propriæ sanctitatis & Enthusiasmi juga declinasse, supra diximus, superstitionem Enthusiasta incrustarunt. Eorum primipili, Nicolaus Ciconia,
units.tr: XVII. Akin to the Gnostics and Libertines are those who are infamous under the name of Strong Spirits [Spirituum fortium], and who in France are also called Deists [Deistæ]. They are not called this in the sense in which Prateolus, in his Elenchus of Heresies, book IV, called the Antitrinitarians and Arians Deists [Deistas]. They are so named by antiphrasis, because they profess to know God perfectly, while they plainly deny his providence, his revelation and his grace, and everything that displeases carnal man. For the same reason they openly deny God himself. So too, of old, generals who had conquered peoples were called Africanus, Germanicus and so on [Africani, Germanici]. Puffed up with pride in their own gnosis [γνώσεως], they grow fierce and, walking in the stubbornness [לב בשררות] of their heart, turning it away from Jehovah their God (Deut. 29:18, 19), they dare to boast of the strength of their wicked spirit. No kind of men is more wicked than this, since they profess that they still hold to God, yet with unclean mouths deny what belongs to God and mock Christian simplicity impiously. They also love to be called Degrues, because, unlike other cranes [grues], who tremble at the mysteries of the Christian religion, they look down on them with haughty brows and mock them with a sardonic laugh. Would that their most sorrowful crop had not choked the field of the Lord, and did not choke it every day! XVIII. Of those later Gnostics, the Messalians, and those whom we said above had turned from the depths of obscene lusts to the heights of a holiness and enthusiasm of their own, the superstition of enthusiasm was encrusted. Among their leaders was Nicolaus Ciconia,

units.la: Thomas Muncerus, Cygneæ primùm, post Alsteræ in collimitio Thuringiæ & Saxoniæ sitæ oppido pastor, cujus auspiciis funesta illa Rusticorum seditio in nervum erupit; Melchior Hofmannus, Monasterienses turbones, & præ omnibus aliis famosus ille David Georgius, Delphensis Batavus, horrendarum blasphemiarum æquè ac propudiosarum libidinum Magister, se pro Christo Dei venditare ausus; Schwenkfeldius, eques Silesius, è Ducatu Lignicensi, aliique, qui absolutam primitus libertatem non à jugo duntaxat Antichristi, sed etiam politico quovis affectantes cùm pro ea præsidium in Scripturis nullum reperissent, ad enthusiasmos, & libertati tali, & novis dogmatibus aliis præsidium certius allaturos, se convertere ausi sunt.
units.tr: Thomas Muncerus, first a minister at Zwickau and then at Allstedt, a town on the border of Thuringia and Saxony, under whose auspices that disastrous peasants' rebellion broke out; Melchior Hofmann; the Münster disturbers [Monasterienses]; and, above all the others, that notorious David Georgius, a Batavian of Delft, master of horrible blasphemies and equally shameless lusts, who dared to pass himself off as Christ of God; Schwenkfeld, a Silesian knight from the Duchy of Liegnitz; and others who, seeking absolute liberty at first not only from the yoke of Antichrist but also from every political yoke, and finding no support for it in Scripture, dared to turn to enthusiasms and to other new dogmas, which they hoped would give them a surer support.

units.la: fantum, & lac parvulorum illuminatis, adultioribus, & perfectioribus quicquam ad exactiorem rerum Cœlestium cognitionem conducere inficiantur. Ablactandos enim esse adultiores natu & grandiores, utpote qui non amplius ψυχικοὶ animales, sed πνευματικοὶ spirituales, in cœtum quodammodo Angelorum admissi, ab ipso fonte veritatis per se, sine Scripturæ verbo, sapientiam longè sublimiorem, abdicatis penitus Scripturis, hauriant. Nota sunt illa adversus Scripturam convitia & scommata, quæ Paradoxorum titulo Sebastianus Francus in Proœmio Paradoxorum 200. palliavit. Litera Scripturæ, sic ille ex mente Enthusiastarum, Antichristi gladius, Christum occidit: Scriptura sine luce vita & interprete Spiritus, obscura lucerna, & occidens litera est: Hæreses & secta ex litera Scripturæ sunt: Vagina est, non gladius spiritus, Silenus Alcibiadis. Scripturæ sic eliminatæ vicem subire Magisterium Spiritus liberrimi intus loquentis, & altiorem longè γνῶσιν atque sapientiam, quàm quæ Scripturis sacris continetur, dictantis, voluerunt juss. Addunt, homini singulare & proprium aliquod Sabbathum, seu quietem animæ frequentandam esse, qua animus omnibus cogitationibus & curis aliis exsolutus, in se ipsum verti, hærere, & cœlestem illum enthusiasmum, seu Numinis afflatum, ceu unicum jam Dei verbum, & spiritum operiri, cúmque dicendorum & faciendorum omnium, sive cum lege Dei scripta conveniant, sive ab ea multùm discrepent, regulam & amussim habere debeat. Denique Spiritu illo actos ita in Deum rapi, ut deificentur, etiam pertendunt. Qui manifestus cum Gnosticis utrisque, Sapientiam & γνῶσιν altiorem, quàm quæ in Scripturis revelata est, sibi arrogantibus, reliquos, ceu Psychicos & umbram, aspernantibus, & sui Deificationem jactantibus, syncretismus est. Neque immerito Lutherus, Zwinglius, Calvinus, de Fanaticis & Enthusiastis ejusmodi questi sunt, quod, cum ipsi fortiter contra Antichristum in prima acie dimicassent, hi spiritibus suis lymphaticis a tergo omnia commiscuerint.
units.tr: fantum, & lac parvulorum illuminatis, adultioribus, & perfectioribus quicquam ad exactiorem rerum Cœlestium cognitionem conducere inficiantur. Translation: ...indeed, and deny that the milk of infants contributes anything to a more exact knowledge of heavenly things for the enlightened, the more mature and the more perfect. For the more advanced and grown-up are to be weaned, as being no longer psychic, animal but pneumatic, spiritual, admitted in some sense into the company of angels, and they draw wisdom far more sublime from the very fountain of truth itself, through themselves, without the word of Scripture, having utterly renounced the Scriptures. Well known are those insults and jeers against Scripture, which Sebastian Franck cloaked under the title of Paradoxes in his preface to the Paradoxes, number 200. "The letter of Scripture," he says, in the mind of the Enthusiasts, "is the sword of Antichrist, which kills Christ"; "Scripture without the light of life and the Spirit as interpreter is a dim lamp and a killing letter"; "heresies and sects come from the letter of Scripture"; "it is a sheath, not the sword of the Spirit"; "a Silenus of Alcibiades." Having thus removed Scripture, they wished the teaching of the most free Spirit speaking within to take its place, dictating a knowledge [γνῶσις] and wisdom far loftier than what is contained in the holy Scriptures. They add that a certain special and proper Sabbath, or rest of the soul, is to be observed by man, in which the mind, freed from all other thoughts and cares, is turned into itself, cleaves to it, and waits for that heavenly enthusiasm or breath of the Deity, as now the only Word and Spirit of God, and that this must have the rule and standard for everything to be said and done, whether it agrees with the written law of God or differs much from it. Finally, they also maintain that those driven by that Spirit are so carried up into God that they are deified. This is plainly a syncretism of both kinds of Gnostics: those who arrogate to themselves a wisdom and knowledge [γνῶσις] higher than what is revealed in the Scriptures, and who despise the rest as psychic and shadowy, and who boast of their own deification. Not without reason Luther, Zwingli and Calvin complained of such Fanatics and Enthusiasts, that while they themselves fought bravely against Antichrist in the front line, these men with their frenzied spirits threw everything into confusion from behind.

units.la: XX. Spirituales inprimis & perfecti cum haberi velint recentiores hi Gnostici, Enthusiastae, mirum non est, caeteros Christianos omnes, seu simplices, animales, literales, ab iis sperni, & petulantibus dicteriis proscindi. Caeterum tantum abest, ut illi his se praeferre, & sibi prae his placere debeant, ut deterior longe eorum conditio manifeste appareat. Hoc enim utrosque interest, quod illorum linguae majori verborum tumore, & sermonis impotentioris aestu turgent, mentesque pluribus vanis imaginationibus, & enormibus deliriis implentur, etiam tum, cum maxime humiles videri volunt, utpote nihil sibi tribuentes, sed omnem γνῶσιν cognitionem, sapientiam & potentiam suam immediate a Deo derivantes. quae certissima & vanissima altioris notitiae & infallibilis viae, ab ea, quam caeteri Mortales terunt, ostentatio est: hi contra & modeste loquuntur, & certae atque exploratae regulae se subjiciunt, & Christi atque Apostolorum fidei tenacius inhaerent, & tranquilliore cum industria, honestiusque vitam suam omnem componunt. Fieri enim non potest, quin is, qui sibi lex est, & spiritus sui prorsus ἀδηλία libidine regitur, pronior longe ad pessima quaeque patranda fit. quod uti Gnosticis veteribus, ita etiam Enthusiastis recentioribus ad flagitiorum omnium licentiam, & temeritatem insignem projectis, accidisse, satis constat.
units.tr: XX. Since these modern Gnostics and enthusiasts especially wish to be considered spiritual and perfect, it is no wonder that they scorn all other Christians, whether simple, natural, or literal, and tear them to pieces with insolent taunts. Yet they have far less reason than they suppose to prefer themselves to these and to take pleasure in themselves, since their condition is plainly much worse. For the difference between the two groups is this: the tongues of the former swell with a greater bombast of words and a more unbridled heat of speech, and their minds are filled with many vain imaginings and monstrous delusions, even when they most want to seem humble, as if ascribing nothing to themselves, but deriving all their knowledge [γνῶσις], wisdom and power immediately from God. This is a most certain and most empty display of a higher knowledge and an infallible way, different from the path that other mortals tread. The others, on the contrary, speak modestly, submit themselves to a certain and tested rule, cling more firmly to the faith of Christ and the Apostles, and order their whole life with a calmer diligence and more honourably. For it cannot be otherwise: whoever becomes a law to himself and is ruled by the utter obscurity [ἀδηλία] of his own spirit is far more inclined to commit all manner of wickedness. It is well established that, as with the ancient Gnostics, so also with the more recent enthusiasts, this led to a licence for every kind of crime and to notorious recklessness.

units.la: XXI. Cum porro ad hominem meliorem se reddendum & convertendum nulla unio accommodata minus sit, quam realis & physica, qualis Deificatio est, certo id argumento est, Enthusiastas homines pessimos omnium, & per immanem saltum a communi sensu & ratione omni desertos esse. Spiritus enim ille, qui omnia creavit, ad regenerandum & reformandum hominem, mentemque ejus ad humilitatem, sui abnegationem, obsequium Dei, fidem in Christum, amorem proximi, obedientiam erga superiores quosvis, & sanctitatem universam, sic satis potens est, licet homo non Deificetur, vel spiritus ille unione hypostatica cum nostro non uniatur magis, quam unitur cum terra, mari, Sole, Luna & astris reliquis naturalibus Divinitus creatis; quae cuncta tamen ille & creavit, & non Deificata licet, potenter regit. Denique universa illa Enthusiastarum impietas Paganismum, Stoicismum inprimis, à Gnosticis olim, & novissimè à Spinoza incrustatum, cui natura Deus est, nec quicquam nisi immediatè à Deo fieri creditur, ex orco revocat. Et convertendorum illorum spes minor longè, quàm Atheorum ipsorum, est, quia inspirationis & Deificationis prætextu rationis & revelationis veræ usui nuntium remiserunt. Ubi enim homines magno cum fastu, & Campano supercilio, solius inspirationis & spiritus sui prætextu, veritatem abnegant, ignorantia isthæc, vel potiùs insania sine speciali gratia Dei, ἀνίατον κακὸν immedicabile malum, per quod non credentes veritati à Deo judicantur, 2. Thess. II 12. merito habetur. Non enim eos, qui à superstitiosa, qua agitantur, intemperie illos liberare contendunt, velut servaturos, sed potiùs velut occisuros aspiciunt.
units.tr: XXI. Furthermore, since no union is less suited to making man better and turning him to good than a real and physical union, such as deification is, this is a sure proof that the enthusiasts are the worst of men, and have fallen by a huge leap from common sense and reason altogether. For that Spirit who created all things is powerful enough, to regenerate and reform man, and to bring his mind to humility, self-denial, obedience to God, faith in Christ, love of neighbour, obedience to all superiors, and universal holiness, even if man is not deified, or if that Spirit is not joined to our nature by a hypostatic union, any more than he is joined to the earth, the sea, the sun, the moon and the other natural stars created by God. Yet he both created all these and, though they are not deified, rules them powerfully. Finally, that whole impiety of the enthusiasts calls back from the grave Paganism, above all Stoicism, which was once encrusted on the Gnostics and most recently on Spinoza, for whom nature is God, and who believe that nothing happens except immediately from God. And the hope of converting them is far smaller than for the atheists themselves, because under the pretext of inspiration and deification they have sent away the use of reason and of true revelation. For when men, with great arrogance and a Campanian scorn, deny the truth under the pretext of inspiration and their own spirit alone, this ignorance, or rather madness, is rightly regarded as an incurable evil [ἀνίατον κακόν] without special grace from God, by which those who do not believe the truth are judged by God, 2 Thess. 2:12. For they do not seek to free from the superstitious intemperance that drives them, as if they would preserve them, but rather look upon them as beings to be destroyed.

units.la: XXII. Cum Enthusiastis paria Pontificii faciunt.
units.tr: XXII. The Papists do the same things as the Enthusiasts.

units.la: Nil dicam de Monachorum & Monialium Enthusiasmis, qui in claustris & cryptis eorum delicias iis faciunt, quia privum & singulare quid sunt. Potius illud est, quòd Papa, ejúsque gnathones idem Magisterium sapientiæ altioris, quod Enthusiastæ, γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ tuentur. Jam olim Calvinus Instr. adv. Libert. cap. 9. Papistarum cum Libertinis (& eadem opera cum Enthusiastis, ea in re cum Libertinis consentientibus) discordem concordiam apricatus est. Utraque secta, inquit, commune habet, ut Scripturam in allegorias transformet, & sapientiam meliorem ac perfectionem meliorem affectet, quàm quæ illa continetur: quod utrique communi consensu hanc Pauli sententiam obtendant, literam occidere, 2. Cor. III. 6. quòd formam novam introducere volunt, qua Scriptura nasus, quod ajunt, cereus fiat, aut instar pilæ sursum deorsúmque agitetur, &c. Hoc enim palam præ se ferunt. Quintinus enim Heduus, Pammelio in Tertull. de Præscript. Annot. 237. laudante & adoptante; Posteri, inquit, (non veteriores certè) grata sanè & perelegantì metaphora Scripturam vocarunt cereum, ejúsque nasum cereum dixere, quia possit ad libitum quocunque flecti. Tam facile enim est, imò facilius ad res profanas & impias probandas detorquere S. Scripturam, quàm facilè est ex pedibus ac semipedibus, aut penthemimeribus Vergilianis epithalamia, seu quidvis aliud in unum cogere. Cosserus quoque in Enchirid. p. 44. Scriptura, inquit, quas nobis in membranis Apostoli reliquerunt, sunt literæ mortuæ, scripta atramento in membrana vel charta, quam si quis vel truncare velit, vel torquere, vel pravis expositionibus corrumpere, nihil sentiat: Sunt instar vaginæ, quæ quemlibet gladium admittit, non modò chalybeum, sed etiam plumbeum, ligneum, æreum. Patiuntur enim se quavis interpretatione trahi.
units.tr: I will say nothing of the enthusiasms of monks and nuns, who make their pleasures in their cloisters and vaults, since those are a peculiar and separate matter. Rather, the point is that the Pope and his flatterers defend the same teaching of higher wisdom that the Enthusiasts do, with bare head [γυμνῇ κεφαλῇ]. Long ago Calvin, in Instr. adv. Libert. cap. 9., pointed out the discordant agreement between the Papists and the Libertines (and, in the same breath, the Enthusiasts, who agree with the Libertines on this point). Each sect, he says, has this in common: they turn Scripture into allegories, and they aim at a better wisdom and a higher perfection than what is contained in it. Both pursue this with one common consent, citing that saying of Paul, "the letter kills" (2 Cor. 3:6), because they wish to introduce a new form, by which Scripture, as they put it, becomes soft as wax, or is tossed up and down like a ball, and so on. For they openly profess this. Quintinus of Autun, with Pamelius praising and adopting him in his note on Tertullian, De Praescriptione, Annot. 237, says: Later writers (certainly not the older ones) have called Scripture wax, with a pleasing and very elegant metaphor, and they have called its nose wax, because it can be bent in any direction at will.
