For it is so easy, or rather easier, to twist Holy Scripture to prove profane and impious things, than it is to gather epithalamia, or anything else, into one piece out of feet, half-feet, or Virgilian penthemimers. Cosserus too, in Enchiridion, p. 44, says: The Scriptures which the Apostles left us on parchment are dead letters, written in ink on parchment or paper. If anyone wishes to mutilate them, twist them, or corrupt them with perverse expositions, they feel nothing. They are like a scabbard, which admits any sword, not only steel but also lead, wood, or bronze. For they allow themselves to be dragged into any interpretation.

units.la: Pontificiorum enthusiasmus colligitur ex eorundem blasphemiis adversus Scripturam, cereanasum cereum.
units.tr: The enthusiasm of the Papists is gathered from their blasphemies against Scripture, the waxen nose.

units.la: Quæ blasphemè nimis dicta nequicquam illi sic purgare conantur, quasi de sola litera à genuino sensu abstracta intelligenda essent. Nemo enim sanus unquam soli nudæ literæ,genuino sensu carenti,canonicam authoritatem asseruit; neque Scriptura nuda & sola litera, genuino sensu carente,definiri potest.
units.tr: They try in vain to excuse these things, said too blasphemously, as if they were to be understood only of the bare letter, detached from the genuine sense. For no sane person has ever asserted canonical authority for the bare letter alone, lacking the genuine sense; nor can Scripture be defined as a naked and bare letter, lacking the genuine sense.

units.la: XXII. Quid verò multris? Ipse Melchior Canus,& Petrus à Soto Magisterium illud sapientiæ altioris, à veteribus Gnosticis, & novellis Enthusiastis, jactatum manifestè tuentur. Indignum erat, ita Canus de Loc.Theol.lib.III. fund.4. loquitur, ut tota Evangelii doctrina, quæ lex est Spiritus & vitæ,mortuis ubique literis committeretur. Servorum & rudium est, cuncta ex præscripto agere. Judæorum ergo sit scripta hæc lex. At filii perfecti jam viri, & in libertatem gratiæ vocati,legem insculptam in cordibus habent. Disertius Petrus à Soto Def.Cath. Fid. cap.36. Illud, inquit, statuatur ut certissimum, quòd hoc scribendi Divina verba atque revelationes consilium ob imperfectionem & infirmitatem humanam est excogitatum à Deo sanctioribus verò & purioribus, aut minùs, aut nullo modo necessarium. Cap. 38. verbi Dei quatuor gradus & genera facit; puta 1. Verbum æternum, immensum & incomprehensibile, de quo Johannes: In principio erat verbum. II. Verbum Dei in cordibus, seu revelationes Prophetarum cordibus à Deo infusas. III. Prædicationem Propheticam & Apostolicam. IV. Scripturam. Secundum, tertium & quartum gradum totidem verbi æterni quasi participationes quasdam & velut femina facit, quæ cum mentes nostræ suscipiunt, atque cogitationes suas & affectus illis subjiciunt, non aliter se habent ad Deum, quàm discipuli ad Magistrum, & quodammodo Deificantur; idque pro gradu & puritate cujusque. Puritatis illius gradus sic cap. 36. explicat: Multò purius & integrius Dei cognitio aut solo verbo, aut interiore tantùm revelatione hominibus participatur. Et sanè quò Divina nobis purgatiora, & ut ita dicam,ab omni similitudine, atque ab omni re corporea magis separata traduntur, signum est purgationis animi, Divinarumque rerum capacioris, & illæ multò perfectius agnoscuntur. Quid his Gnosticum, quid Enthusiasticum magis? Monstrosa inprimis illa, quam pro tertio gradu verbi Dei obtrudunt, participatio æterni verbi,quæ sine ulla imagine & phantasmate, mentium nostrarum Deificatione quadam perficitur; est. Hoc enim expressum illud magisterium Dei,absq; ulla lege,canone & norma,ceu τύπῳ διδαχῆς, docentis, est,quod Enthusiastæ urgent. Et hoc unum Enthusiastas & Pontificios interest, quòd illi suum illud Dei verbum persectissimum,purissimis & maximè spiritualibus quibusvis, etiam idiotis: hi cordi solius Ecclesiæ repræsentativæ,hoc est,Papæ, vindicant.
units.tr: XXII. What more need be said? Melchior Cano and Peter à Soto clearly defend that lofty teaching of wisdom, which was boasted of by the ancient Gnostics and the newer Enthusiasts. "It would be unworthy," Cano says de Loc. Theol. lib. III, fund. 4., "that the whole doctrine of the Gospel, which is the law of the Spirit and of life, should everywhere be entrusted to dead letters. It belongs to slaves and the untaught to do everything by written rule. Let this written law be for the Jews. But the sons, now grown men and called into the liberty of grace, have the law engraved in their hearts." Peter à Soto speaks more plainly, Def. Cath. Fid. cap. 36.: "Let this be held as most certain: that this plan of writing down the divine words and revelations was devised by God because of human imperfection and weakness, and is less necessary, or not necessary at all, for the holier and purer." In cap. 38. he makes four grades and kinds of the word of God, namely: 1. "The eternal, immense and incomprehensible Word, of which John says: In the beginning was the Word." 2. "The Word of God in hearts, or the revelations infused by God into the hearts of the prophets." 3. "Prophetic and apostolic preaching." 4. "Scripture." The second, third and fourth grades he makes, as it were, so many participations in the eternal Word, which, when our minds receive them and subject their thoughts and affections to them, stand toward God no otherwise than disciples toward a teacher, and in a certain way are deified; and this according to the degree and purity of each person." He explains the degree of that purity thus, cap. 36.: "The knowledge of God is shared with men much more purely and completely either by the Word alone or by inner revelation alone. And indeed, the more purely and, so to speak, the more free from all likeness and from every corporeal thing the divine things are handed down to us, the more it is a sign of the purging of the soul and of its greater capacity for divine things, and those things are recognised far more perfectly." What is more Gnostic, what more Enthusiastic than this? Above all, that monstrous thing which they thrust forward as the third grade of the Word of God, "the participation in the eternal Word, which is accomplished without any image or phantasm, by a certain deification of our minds," is such a thing. For this is that express teaching of God, without any law, rule or norm, as it were [τύπῳ διδαχῆς] a form of teaching, which the Enthusiasts press. And this alone is the difference between the Enthusiasts and the Papists: the former assign that most perfect word of God to the purest and most spiritual of anyone at all, even the unlearned; the latter claim it for the heart of the represented Church alone, that is, of the Pope.

units.la: XXIV. Eadem Gnosticorum & Enthusiastarum impietate Theologia Familiae Charitatis, Fratrum Rosea Crucis, Valentini Weigelii, & Behmistarum pallet.
units.tr: XXIV. The Theology of the Family of Love, the Brothers of the Rose Cross, Valentin Weigel and the Behmenists shares the same impiety as the Gnostics and Enthusiasts.

units.la: Familiae Charitatis parens Henricus Nicolai, Amstelodamensis est, qui se primum illuminatum Familiae charitatis seniorem dixit, & Mosi Christoque se praeferre ausus est. In exordio Evangelii Regni sic ille inter alia bacchatur: Henricus Nicolai, gratia & misericordia Dei &c. unctus Spiritu S. in tempore antiquo sacra cognitionis Jesu Christi. Deificatus cum Deo in spiritu amoris ejus: illuminatus Spiritu veritatis caelestis, vera perfecta essentia luce. Kvqiάς inter hominum illorum δόξας est, quod familia illa charitatis, cuivis etiam religioni per simulationem ejus, velut piam & licitam, permixta, sit hominum plane perfectorum & Deificatorum, qui neque peccent amplius, neque a peccato quidquam patiantur, atque ita libere & innocenter inter se vivant, ut ne quidem revelatae aliis nuditatis sua pudere ipsos debeat. Utuntur illi inprimis scriptis libris Sebastiani Franki, quo de Lutherus dixisse fertur, eum omnium hominum oleta perreptasse, & in suo proprio suffocatum esse.
units.tr: Henry Nicolas of Amsterdam was the parent of the Family of Love. He called himself "the first enlightened elder of the Family of Love" and dared to set himself above Moses and Christ. At the beginning of the Evangelium Regni he rants, among other things, as follows: "Henry Nicolas, by the grace and mercy of God, etc., anointed with the Holy Spirit in ancient time with the sacred knowledge of Jesus Christ; deified with God in the Spirit of his love; enlightened by the Spirit of heavenly truth, a true and perfect essential light." The chief [κυριωτάτη] of these men's doctrines [δόξαι] is that the Family of Love, mixed by its dissimulation into any religion as if it were pious and lawful, is a company of men who are wholly perfect and deified. They neither sin any more nor suffer anything from sin, and so they live freely and innocently among themselves that they need not be ashamed even of their nakedness being revealed to others. They chiefly use the writings of Sebastian Franck, of whom Luther is said to have remarked that he had crawled through all the sewers of men and been smothered in his own filth.

units.la: XXV. Abstrusam inprimis & singularem Sapientiam a Fr. Christiano Rosenkreuzio, si credere fas est, nati satique Fratres Roseae crucis praese ferunt.
units.tr: XXV. Abstruse and especially singular wisdom, from Fr. Christian Rosenkreutz, if it is right to believe it, is claimed by the born and bred Brothers of the Rose Cross.

units.la: Parens enim ille, Monachus, nobili familia Germanica oriundus, Anno seculi decimi quarti octogesimo octavo peregrinatione ad sepulchrum Christi instituta, Secreta Secretorum ab Arabibus Aegyptiis, aliisque humanam ac Divinam sapientiam & γνωσιν secretissimam didicisse, & mortuus diutissime latuisse, fingitur. In Epitaphio, quod sero repertum nugantur fratres, inter alia his elogiis mactatur, quod ex nobili atque splendida familia Germania oriundus, Vir sui seculi Divinis revelationibus, subtilissimis imaginationibus, ad caelestia atque humana mysteria & arcana admissus &c. centenario anno non morbo, quem nullum expertus sit, sed Spiritu Dei evocante, illuminatam animam suam Deo creatori suo reddiderit. A suis annos centum viginti abscondita esse, aliaque ejusmodi impudentissime confinxerunt. Neque aliud verborum praetumidorum ampullis, & nugis atque ambagibus suis, quam lapidis Philosophici συνημα occultare visi sunt; cum lapide illo sapientiam Divinam & humanam, & aureum Spiritus S. seculum, quo rerum Divinarum & humanarum notitia ad summam ακμην suam enixura sit, incessurum suaviter somniantes.
units.tr: That founder, a monk of a noble German family, is pictured as having, in the year 1388 when a pilgrimage to the sepulchre of Christ was undertaken, learned from the Egyptian Arabs the Secreta Secretorum and other most secret knowledge [γνῶσιν] of human and divine wisdom, and then, having died, to have lain hidden for a very long time. In the epitaph, which the brothers pretend was only found late, he is extolled with such praises among others: that, sprung from a noble and splendid family of Germany, a man of his age admitted by divine revelations and most subtle imaginings to heavenly and human mysteries and secrets, etc., in his hundredth year, not by a disease, which he never experienced, but with the Spirit of God calling him, returned his illuminated soul to God, his creator. They have shamelessly invented that he was hidden for 120 years, and other such things. Indeed, with the bombast of their inflated words, their trifles and circumlocutions, they seem to conceal nothing but the composition [συνημα] of the philosopher's stone, while sweetly dreaming that with that stone divine and human wisdom and the golden age of the Holy Spirit will come upon us, by which the knowledge of divine and human things will reach its peak [ἀκμήν].

units.la: XXVI. Gnostica impietate Theologiam suam foede Va- lentinus Weigelius, Pastor Zsopaunensis in Misnia, conspurcavit.
units.tr: XXVI. Valentin Weigel, minister at Zschopau in Meissen, foully defiled his theology with Gnostic impiety.

units.la: Is enim, homo stolidus & audax, ex Platone, Trismegisto, Dionysio Areopagita, Muncero, Schwenkfeldio, Taulero, & fumoso atque famoso Paracelso illo inprimis, non ex agro Tigurino, uti nonnemini visum, sed vel Eremo vicina, vel incerta patria oriundo; circa Seculi hujus annum duodecimum ejusmodi Theologiam portentosam parturivit, qua non tantum verborum peregrinorum, & cothurnatorum obscuritate sic cornicatus est, ut, quod de Libertinis Calvinus cap 7. dixit, nihilo plus perspicuitatis in verbis ejus, quàm in avium cantu inveniri potuerit; imitatus in eo Gnosticos, barbaris vocabulis Zoroastris & Magorum veterum imitatione, uti, & arcanam illis vim tribuere suetos, ut merito veteres illos pulsari verbis Apostoli: τὰς δὲ βεβήλως κενοφωνίας (alii codices legunt κενοφωνίας) περιῐστασο, Profanas vocum novitates, vel inanitates vita, 2. Tim. II. 16. coll. cum 1. Tim. VI. 20. autumaverint: sed etiam rerum sublimium, & à vulgi, hominumque animalium & literalium, uti passim eos appellat, captu remotissimorum, tumore cornicum omnium oculos configere conatus est. Ipse Gnosticismum, & ὑπερηφανία καταφρονητὴ pratumida vanitatis suae in Pantepistemone, Pansophia, & studio suo universali impotenter prodidit.
units.tr: For this man, a stupid and bold fellow, born not in the Zurich countryside, as some have thought, but near the desert or of uncertain homeland, drew from Plato, Trismegistus, Dionysius the Areopagite, Müntzer, Schwenckfeld, Tauler, and above all from the smoky and notorious Paracelsus, and around the twelfth year of this century brought forth a monstrous theology of this sort. In it he so croaked like a crow with the obscurity of foreign and bombastic words, that what Calvin said of the Libertines in chapter 7, that there was no more clarity in their words than in the song of birds, could be found in his too. In this he imitated the Gnostics, using barbarous words in imitation of Zoroaster and the ancient Magi, whose words they were accustomed to regard as having secret power. So the ancients were rightly struck by the words of the Apostle: "But shun profane and empty babblings" [τὰς δὲ βεβήλους κενοφωνίας] (other manuscripts read κενοφωνίας), "profane novelties of speech, or empty talk of life," 2 Tim. 2:16, compared with 1 Tim. 6:20. He also tried to dazzle the eyes of everyone with the swelling of crows, far removed from the grasp of the common people and of men he calls, everywhere, animal and literal. He himself betrayed his Gnosticism and his arrogance, a contempt that is the vanity of his swollen pride, in his Pantepistemon, Pansophia, and his universal study.

units.la: In Praefat. sic circulator ille ampullatur: Hoc studium universale, non particulare aliquod est, sed omnia continet, quicquid homines in terra addiscere debent & possunt. Nemo scientia sua, eruditione, sapientia ulterius progredi potest. Primum est in mundo, etiam ultimum erit, verissimum studium, quod veritatem omnem absque errore proponit. Accedite huc, quotquot eruditionem amatis. Passim etiam omnes, qui sectae ejus nomen non dederint, ceu vacuos Spiritu S. adeóque verè Rakim, deprimit; & se solum, consentientésque sibi, Spiritu plenos, adeóque verè Gnosticos esse, jactat. De Scriptura, ejúsque literali & spirituali intelligentia nugas Enthusiasticas & Schwenkfeldianas recoquit. Cognitionis humanae principium non Deum, & revelationem ejusdem, sed hominem ipsum, & semina rerum omnium ei insita, faciens, nullum scibile extrinsecus ei inferri, in eo latere omnia, indéque excitari, cum Platonicis veteribus, pertendit. Quod illud γνῶθι σεαυτὸν, ubique ab eo decantatum, est. Quem in finem illud Trismegisti: Video me in omnibus, & omnia in me; ego sum in mari, & mare in me; ego in Caelo, & Caelum in me; ego in inferno, & infernum in me, lymphaticus ille frequenter celebrat. De cognitionis enim forma & ratione statuit, quòd cognoscens cum cognito idem fiat realiter & essentialiter. Cognoscens, sic ille Confess. cap. 13. scribit, fit unum cum cognito, sciens unum cum scito, intelligens cum intelligibili. Verùm Pseudo-Theologi nolunt ipsi essentialiter Deo unirí uniri. Christus & vita ejus in iis non est essentialiter. De eo loqui & concionari quidem possunt, licet extra ipsum sint. Hoc illorum negotium, opera, tenebrae & condemnatio. Alibi: Studium, inquit, & doctrina nostra dat unionem essentialem, ut discens cum discente unum fiat. Regulam porro cognitionis combinationem contradictoriorum facit. Cum enim in Scriptura & ratione contradictoria multa sint, mentis esse illa non per explicationes & respectus diversitatem, sed, rationi & sensui omni indicto bello, absolute, simpliciter & promiscue componere. Quod stultissimum ejus dogma decumanam ad blasphemias januam aperuit, ut impuro ore impurus ille dogmatistes pronuntiare non dubitaverit, Coelum & infernum, Deum & Diabolum, Christum & Bestiam Apocalypticam idem esse. Quae cuncta, atque iis affinia non pauca, inprimis somnium illud ex eburnea porta de imminente Seculo Spiritus S. fere ad amussim Gnosticorum & veterum Platonicorum dogmatum cusa & excusa esse, res ipsa certe loquitur.
units.tr: In the Preface that charlatan puffs himself up thus: This universal study is not some particular one, but contains everything that men on earth ought and are able to learn. No one can advance further in knowledge, learning, or wisdom. It is the first in the world, and will also be the last, the truest study, which sets forth all truth without error. Come here, all of you who love learning. Everywhere he also belittles all who have not given their name to his sect, as empty of the Holy Spirit, and therefore truly Raka, while he boasts that he alone, and those who agree with him, are full of the Spirit and therefore truly Gnostics. Concerning Scripture and its literal and spiritual understanding, he reheats enthusiastic and Schwenckfeldian trifles. Making the principle of human knowledge not God and his revelation, but man himself and the seeds of all things implanted in him, he maintains with the ancient Platonists that no knowable thing is brought into him from outside, but that all things lie hidden in him and are drawn out from there. This is the "know yourself" [γνῶθι σεαυτόν] sung everywhere by him. To this end that frenzied man often celebrates the saying of Trismegistus: I see myself in all things, and all things in me; I am in the sea, and the sea is in me; I am in heaven, and heaven is in me; I am in hell, and hell is in me. For he holds, concerning the form and manner of knowing, that the knower becomes really and essentially one with the known. In his Confessions, chapter 13, he writes: The knower becomes one with the known, the one who knows with what is known, the one who understands with what is understood. But these pseudo-theologians do not wish to be essentially united to God. Christ and his life are not essentially in them. They can indeed speak and preach about him, even while they are outside him. This is their business, their work, their darkness and condemnation. Elsewhere he says: our study and teaching gives an essential union, so that the learner becomes one with the teacher. Moreover, he makes the rule of knowledge a combination of contradictories. For since many things in Scripture and in reason are contradictory, it is the mind's task to join them together absolutely, simply and indiscriminately, not by explanation and distinction of respects, but with war declared on reason and sense alike. This most foolish dogma of his opened the door to blasphemies, so that that impure dogmatist did not hesitate to pronounce with an impure mouth that heaven and hell, God and the Devil, Christ and the Apocalyptic Beast are the same. All these things, and not a few related to them, above all that dream about the ivory gate and the imminent age of the Holy Spirit, were struck and cast almost exactly to the measure of the dogmas of the Gnostics and the ancient Platonists; the thing itself certainly speaks to this.

units.la: XXVII. Ex Paracelsi & Weigelii Schola Jacobus Böhm, sub initium hujus seculi, natus prope Gorlizum, progenies rustica ex sutore Propheta, & Philosophus Teutonicus λεγόμενος, prodiit. Scripsit ille A. MDCXXIII. Mysterium magnum, quo Weigelianismum fere interpolavit, Mysteria fidei in naturam lumine suo resolvit, Enthusiasmo omnia tribuit, & verbi praeconium promiscuum esse jussit. Addidit Auroraм, librum adeo intricatum, & mysteriis insolentibus luxuriantem, ut infernales tenebras referat, nulli, ac ne authori quidem, uti credere fas est, intellectum. Diabolum magnam Deitatis partem esse, ex essentia quippe Dei Patris satum, blasphemare ausus est. Deus, sic ille, ab aeterno solus: essentia ejus dividitur in tres differentias. Una est mundus igneus, secunda mundus tenebrosus, tertia mundus luminosus. Est tamen una solum essentia inter se; verum una non est altera. Tres illae essentiae sunt similiter infinitae, neque loco, neque tempore conclusae. Qualibet differentia se includit in se, in una essentia, & affectio ejus est desiderium, centrum natura. Talia hominis portentosi oracula sunt, talis γνῶσις est; ex qua, velut ἐν κεφαλῇ ὑφασμα dignoscere licet. Camarinam enim illam movere amplius nil attinet.
units.tr: XXVII. From the school of Paracelsus and Weigel came Jacob Böhm, born near Görlitz at the beginning of this century, a rustic offspring, a shoemaker-prophet, called the German philosopher. In 1623 he wrote the Mysterium magnum, in which he largely adulterated Weigelianism, resolved the mysteries of faith into nature by his own light, attributed everything to enthusiasm, and ordered that the preaching of the Word be made common to all. He added the Aurora, a book so tangled, and so rank with unfamiliar mysteries, that it recalls infernal darkness and is understood by no one, not even, as one may believe, by its author. He dared to blaspheme that the Devil is a great part of the Deity, begotten from the very essence of God the Father. God, so he says, is alone from eternity: his essence is divided into three differences. One is the fiery world, the second the dark world, the third the luminous world. Yet there is only one essence among them; but the one is not the other. These three essences are similarly infinite, enclosed neither by place nor by time. Each difference encloses itself in itself, within one essence, and its affection is desire, the centre of nature. Such are the oracles of this monstrous man; such is his gnosis, from which one may recognise the weaving of the whole "from the head" [ἐν κεφαλῇ ὑφασμα]. For there is no further need to stir up that chamber-pot.

units.la: XXVIII. Duo inprimis genera Gnosticorum sunt, quae Ecclesiam inprimis Anglicanam hodie infestant, Quakerorum, uti appellantur, seu Trementium, & Antinomorum. Et Quakerorum quidem segreges coetus facientium origo ea in tempora incidit, quibus in Anglia, sicut olim in Israele, Rex non fuit, & cuivis licuit, quod libuit.
units.tr: XXVIII. There are two chief kinds of Gnostics, which today especially trouble the English Church: the so-called Quakers, or Tremblers, and the Antinomians. As for the Quakers, the origin of their gatherings in separate assemblies falls in those times when in England, as once in Israel, "there was no king, and everyone did what was right in his own eyes."

units.la: Cunabula enim eorum in Annum hujus seculi quadragesimum nonum, quo Rex Carolus I. immani parricidio per furias hujus feculi, phreneticos & sectarios, e medio sublatus est, incidunt. Author sectæ est Georgius Fox, ex Leiceftrenfis Provinciæ pago Dreton oriundus; qui Divina & Coelesti voce ad novi Evangelii fui præconium fe excitum jactavit, & miraculis etiam illud confirmasse, donóque Prophetico & visionibus inclaruisse ab asseclis perhibetur. Brevi secta in Anglia, non obscuro Cronvvelli in eos favore, invaluit, atque inde in Scotiam, Hiberniam, Belgicam, Galliam, Germaniam, ipsámque Americam fe diffudit; Roberto Barklay per fcripta publica, & Guilhelmo Penn per potentiam favoris, qua in aula Anglicana, Quakerum fe simulans, qui Jesuita personatus fuit, ad modernum usque Regem valuit, obfterricantibus. Parum illud est, quod externo tremore & fremitu lymphantes intemperiem suam illorum nonnulli produnt, & non simplicem ἀπαθεωπίαν præ fe omnes ferunt. In eo enim impietatis illorum cardo consistit, quòd prætextu interni, omnibus hominibus à Deo infusi, & ad falutem sufficientis luminis, & immediatæ inspirationis per intervalla, & nec opinos agitantis, & corpus ad tremorem usque subinde concutientis, nec non spiritualis perfectionis & ἀναμαρτησίας quibusdam saltem obtingentis, aliud Evangelium, alium Christum, aliam spiritualem sapientiam & revelationem, quàm eam, quæ à Christo per Evangelistas & Apostolos in Scripturis revelata est, prædicat, promifcuo omnium spiritu incalescentium præconio divulgat, & à regia in Cœlum via, mediis salutis consequendæ Divinitus revelatis, ipso inprimis vero Jesu Christo & vero Deo, aversos avehit. Paucis ex mente Trementium illorum multa dixit Philaletes ille, qui Dilucidationes in Gerhardi Croefii Historiam Quakerianam hoc ipso anno edidit; quarum in frontispicio sic ille, ex sectæ suæ sententia: Christiana religio, seu vera Pietas consistit non in hujus, vel illius confessionis assensu; aut cum his vel illis consensu; aut ab his vel illis dissensu; sed in Dei in nobis per fidem hypostaticam inhabitatione; nostra carnis & sanguinis Christi participatione; & per Baptismum Spiritus S. directione. Quæ pauca verba implicatiora Gnofticum & Enthusiasticum virus eorum occultant. Pluribus eorum pythonifmum, inspirationum & Enthusiasmorum fraudulentiam, vanam cognitionis mysticarum allegoriarum venditationem, quibus notissimam Christi & totius Evangelii historiam & veram consolationem configunt, intolerandam adversus Ministros Christi amarulentiam, aliáque ejusmodi Cl. Henricus Morus Cantabrigiensis Myst. Piet. lib. X. cap. 13. in apricum produxit.
units.tr: For their cradle falls in the year forty-nine of this century, when King Charles I was removed by an monstrous parricide, through the furies of this age, the frenzied and the sectarians. The author of the sect was George Fox, born in the village of Drayton in the province of Leicester. He boasted that he had been roused by a divine and heavenly voice to proclaim his new Gospel, and it is said by his followers that he confirmed it with miracles and became famous for the gift of prophecy and for visions. Soon the sect spread widely in England, not without the obvious favour of Cromwell towards them, and from there it poured into Scotland, Ireland, Belgium, France, Germany, and America itself, with Robert Barclay spreading it through published writings, and William Penn through the power of favour he had at the English court, where, pretending to be a Quaker though he was really a disguised Jesuit, he held influence down to the present King, with midwives in attendance. It is a small matter that some of these raving people betray their disorder by outward trembling and roaring, and that they all show not a simple apatheia [ἀπαθεωπίαν] in their bearing. The hinge of their impiety lies in this: under the pretext of an inner light, poured by God into all men and sufficient for salvation, and of an immediate inspiration which comes at intervals and stirs the mind without reason, and which from time to time shakes the body even to trembling, and also of a spiritual perfection and sinlessness [ἀναμαρτησίας] granted at least to some, they preach another Gospel, another Christ, another spiritual wisdom and revelation than that which was revealed in the Scriptures by Christ through the Evangelists and Apostles. They spread this with a promiscuous proclamation among men all aflame with the same spirit, and they lead men away from the royal road to heaven, from the means of obtaining salvation divinely revealed, and above all from Jesus Christ himself and the true God. The Philalethes who published his Elucidations on Gerhard Croese's Quaker History this very year has said much in a few words, in line with the opinion of these Tremblers; on the title page he writes, in the sect's own words: The Christian religion, or true piety, does not consist in assent to this or that confession, nor in agreement with these or those, nor in dissent from these or those; but in God's indwelling in us through a hypostatic faith, in our participation in the flesh and blood of Christ, and in the guidance of the Holy Spirit through Baptism. These few words, more tangled, hide their Gnostic and enthusiastic poison. Dr. Henry More of Cambridge has brought into the open at greater length their Pythonism, the fraud of their inspirations and enthusiasms, their empty boasting of mystical allegories by which they obscure the most famous history of Christ and the whole Gospel and its true comfort, their intolerable bitterness against the ministers of Christ, and other things of this kind, in Mysterium pietatis, book 10, chapter 13.

units.la: XXIX. Neque minùs Gnosticismum Antinomi, pietatis & sanctimoniae, fidei in Christum, & cognitionis ejusdem praetextu, aperti vel clandestini hostes incrustarunt. Olim quidem Aetiani, & discipulus eorum Eunomius, qui tempore Epiphanii adhuc superstes fuit, usque adeò, uti Augustinus de Haeres. cap. 54. loquitur, bonis moribus inimicus fuit, ut asseveraret, quòd nihil cuiquam obesset quorumlibet peccatorum perpetratio, ac perseverantia peccatorum, si hujus, qua ab illo docebatur, fidei particeps esset. Quos verbis Christi: Hæc est vita æterna, ut te cognoscant &c. Joh. XVII. 3 abusos esse, ad illum Augustini locum Lambertus Danaeus notavit. Reformationis tempore Johannes Agricola Islebius Anomorum illorum veterum haeresin ex orco revocans, legem, ipsúmque adeò etiam Decalogum praedicandum esse, vel Evangelium non praedicandum esse nisi prius per legem contritis, & quasi satis, severè negavit, & Decalogi praeconium ex pulpitis Ecclesiae ad curiam relegavit. Ausus etiam est Nicolaus Amsdorfius palam asserere, bona opera ad salutem noxia & perniciosa esse. Demum nostro Seculo Gnosticus ille Antinomianismus in Anglia lacertos iterum commovisse visus est, Johanne Eatono, Thoma Crispo, & Johanne Saltmarsh, incentoribus. Eatonus enim libro, de gratuita & libera justificatione per solum Christum, publicato, Deum nec velle, nec posse videre peccata, quae justificati semel committunt, pertendit. Tritae & frequentatae eorum voces sunt, nihil conferre bona opera ad necessitatem salutis; Nec causam regnandi, nec viam ad regnum illa esse: Quicquid boni agimus, non nobis, sed Christo nos agere: Nefas esse quicquam boni agere ea intentione, ut id agendo salutem nostram promoveamus: Nullum virtutis vel sanctimonia efficium esse, quo vel minimum boni lucremur: Exercitium sanctimonia & bonorum operum ne pro idoneo quidem & sufficiente indicio atque argumento habendum esse quod in statu gratiae, & expectatione gloriae simus: Ipsam fidelium sinceram sanctitatem, à Spiritu gratiae profectam, in sui exercitio, sordes & stercus esse coram Deo; ac proin eum, qui tanta, quanta potest, diligentia sanctitati operam dat, nihilo Deo gratiorem vel acceptiorem esse quàm si illam negligeret, vel vitiis indulgeret. Quae φορτικὰ ἀχρήσματα sunt. Licet enim castiorem hominum horum in quibusdam mentem & sensum, quàm verba esse, pridem Celeb. Hoornbekius Summ. Controv. pag. 812. autumaverit, & novissimè Celeb. Witsius in doctissimis & cedro dignis Animadversionibus Irenicis ad controversias, quae sub infaustis Antinomiorum morum & Neonomorum nominibus nunc in Britannia agitantur, emollire plura per dextram interpretationem, & pacificum studium conatus sit; ejusmodi tamen isthæc sunt, ut ea improbare, & obelo sanctiore configere, posterior etiam nullus dubitaverit. Gangræna nam enim hic sermo habet, & præsentissimum pietati, apud vulgus imprimis, quod melioribus consultis, & benignioribus interpretationibus vix unquam studet, vel studere potest, & facile ad carnalia abripitur, venenum infundit; denique ad Gnosticismum, pietati omni, γνώσεως suæ prætextu, bellum indicentem, planam viam sternit. Saluberrima de cætero & sapientissima Celeb. Witsii consilia sunt, quæ diffidentibus Antinomis & Neonomis suggerit, quibus utinam illi vacivas aures substringere dignentur! Non enim Evangelium schola licentiæ est, neque adventus Christi in mundum is finis fuit, ut à Cœlesti Rege secum ferret diploma pro hominibus, quo instructi posthac cum authoritate, vel saltem cum securitate & impunitate peccarent, quasi nihil amplius iis incumbetet, quàm ut credant & profiteantur, Christum pro se mortuum esse. Dedit enim ipsum pro nobis, ut redimeret nos ab omni iniquitate, & purificaret sibi populum peculiarem, ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων æmulum bonorum operum, Tit. II.14.
units.tr: XXIX. Likewise, the Gnosticism of the Antinomians, under the pretext of piety and holiness, of faith in Christ and of knowledge of him, has been taken up by open and secret enemies. Formerly the Aetians, and their disciple Eunomius, who was still alive in the time of Epiphanius, were so hostile to good morals, as Augustine says in his book On Heresies, chapter 54, that they asserted that the commission of any sins whatever, and persistence in sin, does no harm to anyone who shares in the faith taught by them. Lambert Daneau has observed that these men abused the words of Christ, "This is eternal life, that they know you," etc., John 17:3, and cited Augustine's passage against them. At the time of the Reformation, Johann Agricola of Eisleben, recalling from hell the heresy of those ancient Antinomians, flatly denied that the law, or even the Decalogue itself, must be preached, or that the Gospel should not be preached unless men had first been sufficiently crushed by the law; and he banished the proclamation of the Decalogue from the pulpits of the Church to the court. Nicolaus Amsdorf also dared to assert openly that good works are harmful and pernicious to salvation. Finally, in our own century that Gnostic Antinomianism seemed to stir its limbs again in England, with John Eaton, Thomas Crisp and John Saltmarsh as its instigators. For Eaton, in a book published On gratuitous and free justification through Christ alone, maintained that God neither wills nor is able to see the sins which justified men commit. Their worn and frequent phrases are: good works contribute nothing to the necessity of salvation; they are neither the cause of reigning nor the way to the kingdom; whatever good we do, it is not we but Christ who does it in us; it is wrong to do anything good with the intention of promoting our salvation by doing it; no act of virtue or holiness exists by which we could gain even the least good; the exercise of holiness and of good works should not even be held as a fit and sufficient sign and proof that we are in a state of grace and expectation of glory; the sincere holiness of the faithful, proceeding from the Spirit of grace, is in its exercise filth and dung before God; and therefore he who devotes himself to holiness with all the diligence he can is no more pleasing or acceptable to God than if he neglected it or indulged in vices. These are φορτικὰ ἀχρήσματα [vulgar and useless things]. For although the Celebrated Hoornbeeck, in Summa Controversiarum, p. 812, long ago judged that in some of these men the mind and sense are more chaste than their words, and although the Celebrated Witsius, most learned and worthy of cedar, in his Irenic Animadversions on the controversies now being waged in Britain under the unhappy names of Antinomians and Neonomians, has tried to soften many points by a favourable interpretation and a peaceable zeal, yet these statements are of such a kind that no later writer has hesitated to disapprove of them and to mark them with a more sacred obelus. For this kind of speech is a gangrene, and it pours poison into piety, which above all among the common people very rarely or never strives for, or is able to strive for, better judgements and kinder interpretations, and easily is dragged towards the carnal; in short, it lays a plain road for a Gnosticism that declares war on all piety under the pretext of its own knowledge. Otherwise, the most wholesome and wise counsels are those which the Celebrated Witsius offers to the disaffected Antinomians and Neonomians; would that they deigned to open their empty ears to them! For the Gospel is not a school of licence, nor was the coming of Christ into the world meant to bring from the heavenly King a warrant for men, by which, equipped thereafter with authority, or at least with security and impunity, they might sin, as if nothing more were incumbent on them than to believe and profess that Christ died for them. For he gave himself for us, that he might redeem us from all iniquity and purify for himself a peculiar people, zealous of good works [ζηλωτὴν καλῶν ἔργων], Titus 2:14.

units.la: XXX.
units.tr: XXX.

units.la: Superstunt Mystici recentiores, quos idem Gnosticorum, perinde ut vetustiores illos, de quibus supra diximus, virus adflavit. Ipsa Mysticorum vox syncretismum cum Gnosticis prodit, quia non vulgaribus mysteriis, qualia Deus in Scripturis revelavit, sed altioribus longè, fidelium promiscuorum turbæ minimè competentibus, sed paucioribus selectis, purgatis, illuminatis, & Deo unitis, ejusque essentiam contemplantibus, & in contemplatione ea secure indormientibus, perinde ut veteres Gnostici, intumescunt. Mysticam eam Theologiam Thomas à Jesu de Contempl. Div. lib. V. 12. ita vocari monet, non quia mysticum Scripturæ sensum à literali distinctum eruit, sed quia & arcana & occulta Dei notitia est, utpote quæ in caliginosa & occulta cognitione consistat. Sandæus verò Theol. Myst. lib. I. p. 6. eam definit, quòd sit Notitia contemplativa Sapida Dei ac Divinorum. Non nudè notitiam, qualis in Scholastica etiam, symbolica, omnique alia Theologia inest, sed notitiam contemplativam, arctato nomine ad Mysticam à cæteris distinctam; & sapidam, quia contemplatio ejusmodi in voluntate singularem delectationem pariat; eámque versantem circa Deum, ejus inprimis essentiam, non quatenus purè intelligibilis, sed quatenus amabilis est, adeóque sub ratione non purè speculativa, sed practica, quia contemplationis mysticæ finis unio cum Deo est; & Divina, attributa videlicet Dei, qualia Claudius Aquaviva, Generalis Societatis Jesu, lib. de Renov.Spir. & Correspcum Deo, duodecim enumerat; insignit. Discors tamen in his Mysticorum concordia est,uti Sandæus idem pluribus ostendit,& ex iis,quæ dicturi sumus,liquebit.
units.tr: There remain the more recent Mystics, whom the same poison of the Gnostics has breathed upon, just as it did those older ones of whom we spoke above. The very word Mystic betrays a syncretism with the Gnostics, for they puff themselves up over not the common mysteries, such as God has revealed in the Scriptures, but far higher ones, which are by no means suited to the crowd of the faithful at large, but to a few chosen, purified, enlightened men united with God, who contemplate his essence and sleep securely in that contemplation, just as the ancient Gnostics did. Thomas à Jesu, in On Divine Contemplation, book 5, chapter 12, advises that this theology be so called, not because it draws out a mystical sense of Scripture distinct from the literal, but because it is a hidden and secret knowledge of God, consisting in a dark and obscure cognition. Sandaeus, however, in Mystical Theology, book 1, p. 6, defines it as a contemplative, savoury knowledge of God and of divine things. He does not say simply knowledge, such as is found also in Scholastic, symbolic and every other theology, but contemplative knowledge, the name being narrowed to mark off the Mystical from the rest; and savoury, because contemplation of this kind produces a singular delight in the will; and it is concerned with God, above all with his essence, not as it is purely intelligible but as it is lovable, and so under an aspect not purely speculative but practical, since the end of mystical contemplation is union with God; and it is marked as divine with the attributes of God, which Claudio Acquaviva, General of the Society of Jesus, in his book on the renewal of the spirit and on being with God, enumerates as twelve. Yet there is a discordant harmony among these Mystics, as Sandaeus himself shows at length, and it will become clear from what we are about to say.

units.la: XXXI. Theologiam nempe illam studiosissimè omnium nostra ætate Michael de Molinos, Hispanus, ex Aragoniæ Regno oriundus, Theol.Doct. Sacerdos & Concionator Neapolitanus, famosus ille sectæ Quietistarum author,excoluit; non contemnendas in Hispania, Italia, Romæ inprimis, Gallia, alibique partes nactus. Edidit enim ille A.MDCLXXV. librum, cui Manuductionis spiritualis, extricantis animam, eámque per viam interiorem ad acquirendam perfectionem contemplationis, ac divitem pacis interioris (sive quietis mysticæ) thesaurum deducentis, titulum fecit. Quo libro varias in linguas transfuso, & à Jacobo Archiepiscopo Panormitano, & Inquisitionis Qualificatore, uti vocant,non uno, probata & amplissimè commendata, Cardinalis quinetiam Petruccii, cui ipse Papa Innocentius XI. non obscurè favere visus est, suffragium promerito, mysteria sua plenè planéque reseravit. Summa eorum huc redit: Animam, via interna incessuram, nihil operando annihilare se debere, fierique corporis instar mortui; adeóque nec cogitare de ulla re, sive salute aeterna, sive peccatis, horúmque poenis, nec velle, nec agere, nec sentire quicquam. Deum enim solum in nobis absque nobis agere velle; huic omnem de nobis cogitationem relinquendam esse. Nihil petendum esse, quia petere est velle, ut Deus non suam, sed nostram voluntatem exequatur, atque dum homo orat & petit a Deo, Diabolus efficiat, ne Deus animam alloquatur. Licet ore preces recitentur, non tamen opus esse, ut ea ab anima suis meditationibus, aut ratiocinationibus adjuventur. Nec fidem requiri, nisi obscuram & generalem, non autem distinctam attributorum Dei & Trinitatis notitiam complexam. Non excitandam esse devotionem nostram, quin semper redeundum esse ad nihilum suum, & permanendum esse in quiete imperturbabili, ac resignatione passiva. Si forte ante, vel post communionem sacram motus quidam humiliationis, petitionis, gratiarum actionis sentiri occipiant, sedandos ilico esse. Boni ominis esse, si anima discursus de Deo & virtutibus fastidiat, ac ne orationem quidem Dominicam recitare possit. Viæ internæ nihil negotii cum confessione, confessariis, casibus conscientiæ, Theologia & Philosophia intercedere. Animabus mystice mortuis Deum impossibilem reddere consessionem, ipsumque ejus, & poenitentia defectum per gratiam praeservantem, duplo majorem, supplere. Perveniri hac via ad mortem mysticam sensuum, animamque redire ad quietem, principiumque suum, essentiam nempe Divinam, in qua (divinizata) Deificata maneat. Olim Deum Sanctos fecisse per martyria & tyrannos; hodie per Diabolos, qui physice adigunt corporis membra ad actus venereos, atque flagitiosos alios. Hac enim via hominis illuminationem, perfectionem & unionem cum Deo procedere. Incitet interim Sathan, sentiat natura, cogatur corpus facere, quicquid Sathanas voluerit, nil interesse, dum anima intus nec consentiat, nec resistat, nisi resistentia negativa, nec inquietetur ipsius natura, aut corpus facere coguntur, sed resignata maneat. Utrum autem haec vel illa anima sponte peccet, an per violentias Diabolicas actum exerceat, ex lumine actuali Divinitus dato cognosci posse. Denique animam his sublatis intrare in se, in purum centrum suum, ubi Dei imago, merus amor, mera quies, merum silentium, oblivio rerum omnium, & perfecta sui Deo traditio sit; ibi animam audire Deum, cum eo loqui, essentiam ejus per intuitum fixum contemplari, cum voluntate Dei confirmari, neque amplius animam vivere, sed Deum in illa vivere; eamque phoenicis instar renovari, transformari, & Deificari.
units.tr: XXXI. That theology was cultivated most eagerly of all in our age by Michael de Molinos, a Spaniard born in the kingdom of Aragon, a Doctor of Theology, priest and preacher at Naples, the famous author of the sect of the Quietists, who won no contemptible following in Spain, Italy, above all Rome, France and elsewhere. For in 1675 he published a book entitled A Spiritual Guide, which disentangles the soul and leads it by the inner way to acquire the perfection of contemplation and the rich treasure of inner peace (or mystical quiet). This book was translated into various languages, was approved and most highly commended by Jacopo, Archbishop of Palermo, and by more than one Qualifier of the Inquisition, as they are called, and was given the support it deserved from Cardinal Petrucci, whom Pope Innocent XI himself seemed not obscurely to favour; and in it he fully and plainly unlocked his mysteries. The sum of them comes to this: The soul, entering the inner way, must annihilate itself by doing nothing, and become like a dead body; so it must not think of anything, whether eternal salvation or sins and their punishments, nor will, act, or feel anything. For God alone, without us, wills and acts in us; all thought of ourselves must be left to him. Nothing is to be asked for, because to ask is to will, that God should carry out not his own will but ours; and while a man prays and asks of God, the Devil brings it about that God does not address the soul. Although prayers are recited with the mouth, it is not necessary that the soul be helped in them by its own meditations or reasonings. Nor is faith required, except an obscure and general one, not a distinct and complex knowledge of the attributes of God and of the Trinity. Our devotion must not be stirred up, but we must always return to our own nothingness and remain in imperturbable quiet and passive resignation. If perhaps before or after holy communion some movements of humiliation, petition or thanksgiving begin to be felt, they must be quieted at once. It is a good sign if the soul is weary of discourse about God and the virtues, and cannot even recite the Lord's Prayer. The inner way has nothing to do with confession, confessors, cases of conscience, theology or philosophy. To make confession impossible to mystically dead souls, and to supply the defect of that confession and of penitence by a grace that preserves them, is twice as great a thing. By this way one arrives at the mystical death of the senses, and the soul returns to quiet and to its principle, namely the Divine essence, in which it remains deified. Formerly God made the saints through martyrdoms and tyrants; today he does so through Devils, who physically drive the members of the body to venereal and other shameful acts. For by this way the illumination, perfection and union of man with God proceeds. Meanwhile let Satan incite, let nature feel, let the body be compelled to do whatever Satan wills; it makes no difference, provided the soul within neither consents nor resists, except with a negative resistance, and its nature is not disturbed, nor is the body compelled to act, but the soul remains resigned. Whether this or that soul sins of its own accord, or exercises an act under Diabolical violence, can be known from the actual light divinely given. Finally, with these things removed, the soul enters into itself, into its pure centre, where there is the image of God, pure love, pure quiet, pure silence, forgetfulness of all things, and perfect surrender of self to God; there the soul hears God, speaks with him, contemplates his essence by fixed intuition, is confirmed with the will of God, and no longer lives itself, but God lives in it; and it is renewed like the phoenix, transformed and deified.

units.la: XXXII.
units.tr: XXXII.

units.la: Ex his, quid monstri Quietissimus mysticus Molinosii, multum a vetustiore Theologia Mystica discedentis, ad liquidum perducitur. Nil enim nisi Gnosticam luem, enthusiasmos, Deificationem hominis, seu metamorphosin ejus in essentiam Dei, & unionem cum eadem per γνῶσιν contemplationem ejus perfectissimam, non per elevationem mentis in Deum suspensae, sed per intuitum fixum, qualem Segnerus Jesuita in Concordia laboris & quietis incantationi aequiparare non dubitat; ἀδιαφορίαν, impeccantiam, in quibus cunctis Gnosticae impietatis τὸ ἄχρον confisitur, spirat & redolet. Et rite cuncta reputando, facile inducor ut credam, omnes ejusmodi Fanaticorum γνώσεις, speculationes, Deificationes & enthusiasmos, veterum paganismum, Stoicismum inprimis, cui Natura, & quaecunque in natura sunt, Deus sunt, ex orco revocare. Nam etiam Spinoza, qui palam Stoicismum incrustavit, & Naturam pro Deo venditavit, explosio verbo Dei externo, non aliunde magis, quam a verbo quodam interno & enthusiasmo praesidium atheismo suo mutuari potuit.
units.tr: From these points it becomes plain what monstrosity the Quietissimus of Molinos is, a mystic who departs far from the older mystical theology. For it breathes nothing but Gnostic plague, enthusiasm, the deification of man, or his transformation into the essence of God and union with it through γνῶσις [knowledge], a most perfect contemplation of God. This contemplation comes not from the mind being raised up to God but through a fixed intuition, which Segner the Jesuit, in his Concordia laboris & quietis, does not hesitate to equate with incantation. It also breathes and smells of ἀδιαφορία [indifference] and impeccability, in which the extreme of Gnostic impiety is wholly rooted. Weighing everything properly, I am easily led to believe that all such γνώσεις [knowledges], speculations, deifications and enthusiasms of these fanatics call back from the dead the paganism of the ancients, above all Stoicism, for which Nature, and whatever is in nature, is God. Indeed Spinoza too, who openly plastered over Stoicism and hawked Nature as God, once he had rejected the external word of God, could borrow the protection for his atheism from nothing else so much as from some inner word and enthusiasm.

units.la: XXXIII.
units.tr: XXXIII.

units.la: Possemus & alios Gnosticorum complices inducere. Sed sufficient abunde, quos integris sectis disparatos hactenus citavimus. Hoc solum monuisse operae pretium fuerit, in ipso Ecclesiæ gremio non deesse, apud quos per nescio quam ἀμετρίαν τῆς ἀνθολκῆς cognitio Divinarum rerum arida, à praxi pietatis & à fine suo, extra quem terrena, animalia & daemoniaca est, Jac. III. 15. secreta, & divulsa utramque religionis paginam faciat. Qui etiam, perinde ac si in Gnosticorum & Antinomorum castra transeundum nobis esset, pietatis in veritate & mysteriis fidei latentis anxiam scrutationem & μοῦσφων vix æquo animo ferunt. Non desunt etiam qui Scripturæ sensus mysticos, à literali divulsos, sectati, & terminos etiam mysticos ἀγεφῶς temerè & inconsiderate adoptantes, singularem, & à vulgi captu remotam sapientiam comminiscantur, δοκησισοφίαν suam ostentent. Alii Theologiam Scholasticam, meretriculam illam Sophisticam, cum vera & saniore Theologia commiscentes, & ἀσύγκλωστα συγκλώθοντες speculationibus suis in tanti momenti rebus æquo nimium indulgent, & in iis, procul amandata unicè necessaria cognitione, quæ secundum pietatem est, omnem ferè ætatem conterunt. Theologiæ enim unicè salutaris, quæ ex solo Dei verbo, cum manifestatione veritatis ejus ad omnem conscientiam, peti, concinnari & ad architectonicum finem suum unicè referri debuerat, loco à multis pridem exculta est scientia artificiosa, seu μικροφιλοσοφοθεολογία, cui Philosophia non tam ancillatur, quàm dominatur, & captivæ instar nequiter insultat. Ubi enim Philosophia menti expoliendæ, & facultatum intellectualium usui, exercitio, confirmationi inservit; ubi divinæ sapientiæ, & potentiæ in rerum naturis characterum impressorum vestigia perscrutatur, sapientiæ omni, ipsíque adeò Theologiæ ancillari rectè dicitur. Verùm spinosissimarum quæstionum de rebus ad Dei salutarem cognitionem nihil pertinentibus in fines Theologiæ traductio, & cum eadem ἀθέμιτῳ μίξις, veritatis spiritualis terminorum subtilium catenis & vinculis constrictæ depressio; mentis ipsius, vanissimarum ratiocinationum habitu introducto, præjudicatio, quæ inter alia innumera mala usum ejus comitantur, non famulatus, sed dominationis notæ sunt. Neque adeò, frigescente salutari cognitione, quæ secundum pietatem est, mirum est, paucos in rerum cœlestium admirationem & amorem exardescere, ac ne eo quidem affectu erga eas abripi, quo Philosophos veteres erga suam illam tenuem & obscuram veritatis umbram abreptos constat. Ejus enim tantus amor, tanta admiratio illos cepit, ut haud raro in contemplatione ejus ἐκστῶν passi sint. Cùm tamen veritatis naturalis, qui iis illuxerunt, ra-
units.tr: We could bring forward other accomplices of the Gnostics as well. But those whom we have so far cited, scattered among whole sects, will be ample. It will be worth while to point out only this: within the very bosom of the Church there are not lacking those among whom a dry knowledge of divine things, cut off from the practice of piety and from its end (outside of which lie earthly, animal and demonic things, Jas. 3:15), through some sort of ἀμετρία τῆς ἀνθολκῆς [immoderate drawing up] makes secret and tears apart the two pages of religion. These men, as if we had to pass over into the camp of the Gnostics and Antinomians, can scarcely bear with equanimity the anxious search for piety in the truth and in the mysteries of the hidden faith, and its μουσφων [muffled murmuring]. There are also those who, pursuing mystical senses torn away from the literal sense, and adopting rashly and thoughtlessly even mystical terms without distinction, devise a peculiar wisdom far removed from the grasp of the common people, and display their δοκησισοφία [pretended wisdom]. Others, mingling Scholastic theology, that harlot of the sophists, with true and sounder theology, and joining together things that cannot be joined (ἀσύγκλωστα συγκλώθοντες), indulge overmuch in their speculations on matters of such great importance, and in them spend almost their whole lives, setting aside the one necessary knowledge, which is according to godliness. For in place of the one saving theology, which ought to have been gathered solely from the word of God, with the manifestation of its truth to every conscience, and referred solely to its architectonic end, there has long since been cultivated by many an artificial learning, or μικροφιλοσοφοθεολογία [petty philosophical theology], over which Philosophy does not so much serve as handmaid as rule, and insults it wickedly like a captive. For where Philosophy serves to refine the mind and to the use, exercise and strengthening of the intellectual faculties, where it inquires into the traces of divine wisdom and power impressed on the natures of things, it is rightly said to be the handmaid of all wisdom, and of theology itself. But to carry the most thorny questions about things that have nothing to do with saving knowledge of God into the fields of theology, and to mix these with it unlawfully (ἀθέμιτος μίξις), to crush the spiritual truth under the chains and bonds of subtle terms, and to introduce into the mind the habit of most vain reasoning, which is prejudgment: these, among the countless other evils that accompany them, are marks not of service but of domination. Nor indeed, when saving knowledge, which is according to godliness, has grown cold, is it surprising that few are kindled to admiration and love of heavenly things, or that they are not even carried away by that affection toward them with which the ancient philosophers are known to have been carried away toward their own thin and obscure shadow of truth. For such great love and such great admiration seized those men that they often suffered ἐκστασις [ecstasy] in its contemplation. Yet the rays of natural truth that shone upon them, compared with the most profound mysteries of that truth which that Progress from the bosom of the Father, who is the way, the life and the truth (John 14:6), has revealed to us, stand in relation to them hardly otherwise than the twinkling of the tiniest star at night stands to the noonday rays of the sun. All these things, taken together, show traces of a certain racism among those who pursue a dry knowledge and mystical senses torn from the literal sense, and who mix Scholastic theology and philosophy with sounder theology. No good man will deny that these things in some measure recall that ψευδώνυμος γνῶσις [falsely named knowledge], which, as we said above, the Apostle condemned in the Gnostics and in all their followers (1 Tim. 6:20), or at least pave the way to it.

units.la: cismi ve-stigia quædam apud eos, qui cognitionem aridam, sensus mysticos à literali divulsos, sectantur, & Theologiam Scholasticam & Philosophiam Theologiæ saniori commiscent, extant. radii comparati cum profundissimis veritatis illius,quæ nobis è finu Patris progressus ille, qui via, vita & veritas est, Joh.XIV.6. patefecit, mysteriis, vix aliter se habeant, quàm cum solis radiis meridianis nocturna minutissimæ stellæ scintillatio se habet. Quæ cunčta ψευδώνυμον γνῶσιν falsò cognominatam cognitionem illam,quam in Gnosticis, eorumque quibusvis sectatoribus Apostolum, 1.Tim.VI.20. condemnasse, supra diximus, quodammodo respipere, vel ad eam saltem viam sternere,nemo bonus inficias iverit.
units.tr: (Continuation of the same paragraph: the faint marks of this error are found among those who pursue dry knowledge and mystical senses torn from the literal sense, and who mix Scholastic theology and philosophy with the sounder theology. The rays of natural truth that shone upon the ancients, compared with the deepest mysteries of truth which the Son disclosed to us from the Father's bosom, are scarcely otherwise related than the twinkling of a tiny night star to the rays of the midday sun.)

units.la: XXXIV. Missis Gnosticis ad GNOSIMACHOS venimus.
units.tr: XXXIV. With the Gnostics dismissed, we come to the GNOSIMACHI.

units.la: Ipsa nomina indicant,hos illis oppositos fuisse. Sicut enim illos τῦ-Φ© γνώσεως typhus cognitionis & sapientiæ: ita hos τῦΦ© ζηλωτικὸς typhus Zeli,& pietatis singularis, sapientiam & cognitionem abdicantis,imò ei hostiliter adversantis, inflavit. Primus,quod sciam,eorum Johannes Damascenus, Manzur, seu Chrysorrheas dictus, qui A. DCCXXX. claruit, mentionem fecit lib.de Hæres. ubi sic ille: Gnosimachi, inquit, sunt, qui omni Christianorum cognitioni ac scientiæ ita adversantur, ut vanum & minus necessarium laborem esse dicant eorum,qui in Divinis scriptis aliquam exquirunt scientiam. Neque enim Deum aliud à Christiano postulare,nisi præclaras bonásque actiones. Itaque aliquem rudi simplicique animo institutum suum persequi melius est, ut ajunt,quàm multam curam in cognoscendis decretis atque sententiis ponere. Quæ totidem verbis Theodorus Studita,archimandrita doctissimus,qui A.DCCCXXVI.obiit, in epistola ad Athanasium Monachum,hæreseos Mœchianorum propugnatorem,quam Baronius A.809. §.30.recitat, repetiit.
units.tr: The very names show that these were opposed to those. For just as the Gnostics were puffed up with a typhus of knowledge and wisdom (τῦφος γνώσεως), so these were inflated with a typhus of zeal (τῦφος ζηλωτικός), and of peculiar piety, which renounces wisdom and knowledge, or rather is hostilely opposed to them. The first of them, so far as I know, was John of Damascus, called Manzur or Chrysorrhoas, who flourished in 730, and he mentioned them in his book on heresies, where he speaks thus: The Gnosimachi are those who are so opposed to all knowledge and learning among Christians that they say that the labour of those who seek some knowledge in the divine writings is vain and less necessary. For God asks nothing of a Christian but excellent and good actions. Therefore it is better, as they say, to pursue one's duty with a simple and untutored mind than to spend much care on learning the decrees and sentences. Theodore the Studite, a most learned archimandrite, who died in 826, repeated these same words in totidem verbis in his letter to Athanasius the Monk, a defender of the Moechian heresy, which Baronius cites in the year 809, section 30.

units.la: XXXV. Quis Gnosimachorum horum author proximus fuerit,non liquet. Nil enim Ecclesiæ historia eam in rem prodidit. Cæterum eorum Patriarchæ haud dubiè fuerunt Pharisæi, imò vetustiores iis Operarii & Justitiarii, qui hominem propriis operibus & justitia justificari & salvari contendentes,opera & justitiam hominis inde ab incunabulis Ecclesiæ vel planè à vera fide & cognitione Dei separarunt, vel huic longè anteposuerunt. Cujus rei genuina causa est, quòd homines natura gloriam hominum magis quàm Dei diligunt,atque ideo libentius opera faciunt, ut spectentur ab hominibus; quódque φίλαυτοι iidem cùm sint, se potius atque opera & justitiam suam, quàm Deum & justitiam Dei, salutis suæ fabros esse,volunt,& sua Deo imputare amant. Hinc error ille,quòd universa religionis summa, vel saltem principalis ejus pars in praxi, & morum atque virtutum doctrina consistat, tam agnatus gratúsque ho- GNOSIMACHORUM historia. Eorum Patriarchæ Pharisæi & vetustiores iidem, Justitiarii sunt. homini naturali est,quàm ferro rubigo est. Neque alia causa est,quòd populo conciones practicæ,uti vocant,& Ethicæ, longè magis,quàm quæ de mysteriis fidei agunt,allubescnnt. Nam quæ religionis pars de moribus & virtutibus agit, omnibus hominibus accommodata, atque ita conformis rationi est, ut etiam citra revelationem Divinam persuaderi hominibus possit. Neque labore exercito, vel institutione anxia opus est, ut plebs comprehendat, unicuique tribuendum esse, quod suum est, honestè vivendum, neminem lædendum esse,& si quæ ex his conclusa alia ad mores pertinent.
units.tr: XXXV. Who was the nearest author of these Gnosimachi is not clear. For Church history has handed down nothing on the matter. Yet their patriarchs were undoubtedly the Pharisees, and even older than them the Operarii and Justitiarii, who contended that man is justified and saved by his own works and righteousness, and who from the very beginnings of the Church either entirely separated the works and righteousness of man from true faith and knowledge of God, or set them far above it. The genuine cause of this is that men by nature love the glory of men more than the glory of God, and therefore more willingly do works so that they may be seen by men; and that, since they are self-lovers (φίλαυτοι), they wish themselves, their works and their righteousness, rather than God and the righteousness of God, to be the makers of their salvation, and love to impute their own to God. Hence that error, so kin to and so pleasing to the natural man, as rust is to iron: that the whole sum of religion, or at least its principal part, consists in practice and in the doctrine of morals and virtues. [GNOSIMACHORUM historia. Eorum Patriarchæ Pharisæi & vetustiores iidem, Justitiarii sunt. (Running head: History of the Gnosimachi. Their patriarchs are the Pharisees, and the older ones are the same, the Justiciaries.)] Nor is there any other reason why the people are far more delighted with sermons that are, as they call them, practical and ethical, than with those that treat of the mysteries of faith. For the part of religion that treats of morals and virtues is suited to all men, and is so in agreement with reason that it can be persuaded to men even without divine revelation. Nor does the common people need trained labour or anxious instruction to grasp that each should be given what is his own, that one should live honourably, that no one should be harmed, and whatever other conclusions are drawn from these that pertain to conduct.

units.la: XXXVI. Plerasque hæreses Philosophis & Judæis refer- endas acceptas esse, vix dubitari potest.
units.tr: XXXVI. It can hardly be doubted that most heresies are to be traced back to the philosophers and the Jews.

units.la: De Judæis sic Nahum: Exhæresei ote exivit cogitans malum contra Jehovam, יעץ בליעל consiliarius Belialis mnes exorte sunt; ex seu nequitia, Nah.I.11. Sicut igitur salus ex Judæis est, Joh.IV.22 ita Sadducæis haereses fere omnes, & Antichristiana consilia contra Regnum Dei Gnostici; originem suam Judæis debent. Tempore Christi famosæ præ cæteris Pharisæorum & Sadducæorum hæreses fuerunt,quæ pridem anteeum celebre nomen habuerunt. Quibus,ad Tribarefium constituendum,Essenos Scaliger,Drusius, aliíque, addiderunt,quibus cum maledico Serario de iisdem acris contentio fuit. Sicut autem cum Gnosticis veteribus & recentioribus quodammodo conveniunt Sadducæi, qui melioris vitæ spe sublata, & pretio virtuti, atque pœnis peccato detractis,veram solidamque pietatem pensi non habuerunt,& solutiorem vitam traduxerunt: ita cum Gnosimachus tum Esseni,rum Pharisæi paria fecerunt. De Essenis, Synagogæ sectariis, sic Philo Judæus lib.quòd omnis probus liber sit,loquitur: Ἐσι δὲ ... Nec Palæstina Syriaque dresi hoc genus hominem virtutem sectantium, cujus regionis non parvam partem populosa Judæorum gens incolit. In his quidam nominantur Essæi, circiter quatuor millia, παρώνυμοι ὁσιότητος dicti à sanctitate, quia summa religione Deo serviunt, non mactando victimas, sed suas ipsorum mentes ἱεροπρεπεῖς ad sanctimoniam componendo. &c. Τὸ Θεῖον ἐν μάλα Ἀρμενίοις. In solis moralibus se exercent, sub padotribis legibus patriis, quas non potest concipere humanus animus ἄνευ καταχωρίς ἐνθεος sine afflatu Numinis, &c. Discunt sanctitatem, justitiam, curam rei domesticæ vel publicæ, verorum bonorum,malorumque scientiam, atque rerum indifferentium insuper, quid expetendum, quid fugiendum, quæ triplici regula examinant,amore Dei,virtutis & hominum, &c. Eosdem Essenos Eusebius Ἀσκητὰς Ascetas appellat. Sic enim ille Hist.Eccl. lib.II. 17. Βίον τῶν παρ' ἡμῖν ἀσκητῶν ἰσορῶν. Ascetarum
units.tr: Concerning the Jews, Nahum says: "Out of you has come forth one who plots evil against Jehovah, a counsellor of Belial" [יעץ בליעל], Nah. 1.11. Just as salvation is from the Jews (John 4.22), so almost all the heresies of the Sadducees, and the anti-Christian designs against the kingdom of God, the Gnostics, owe their origin to the Jews. In the time of Christ the Pharisees' and Sadducees' heresies were more notorious than the rest, and they had held a famous name long before that time. To these, in constructing their Trihaeresium, Scaliger, Drusius and others added the Essenes, and on this matter there was a sharp dispute between them and the slanderous Serarius. But just as the Sadducees in some respects agree with the ancient and more recent Gnostics, since they abandoned the hope of a better life, removed the rewards of virtue and the punishments of sin, did not take true and solid piety into account, and lived a looser life, so the Pharisees and the Essenes made common cause with the Gnostics. Concerning the Essenes, sectaries of the Synagogue, Philo the Jew speaks thus in his book That Every Good Man Is Free: "...Nor is Palestine, nor Syria, without this kind of men who pursue virtue, and a populous Jewish nation inhabits no small part of that region. Among them are some called Essaeans, about four thousand, called parōnymoi hosiotētos [παρώνυμοι ὁσιότητος], from holiness, because they serve God with the highest devotion, not by sacrificing victims, but by preparing their own minds [ἱεροπρεπεῖς] to be holy..." etc. "...They exercise themselves in moral matters only, under the ancestral laws, which the human mind could not conceive without divine inspiration [ἄνευ καταχωρίς ἐνθεος], etc. They learn holiness, justice, care of domestic and public affairs, the knowledge of true goods and evils, and also of indifferent things: what is to be sought and what avoided; they test these by a threefold rule: love of God, of virtue and of men," etc. Eusebius also calls these same Essenes Ascetae [Ἀσκητάς]. For thus he writes in Ecclesiastical History, book 2, chapter 17: "Looking at the life of our ascetics [ἀσκητῶν]."

units.la: Ex Judaeis exor-tae sunt; ex Sadducæis Gnostici; ex Essenis, Ascetis Judæorum, nostrorum (Essenorum) vitam Philo describit. Ασκηταὶ autem veteribus illi dicti sunt, qui strictius quoddam vitæ genus sectati sunt, voce à Philosophis accepta, quibus exercitatio virtutis & abstinentiæ ἀσκήσεως nomine venit. Ita apud Arianum lib. III. Dissert. caput est ὡξὶ ἀσκήσεως; & apud Artemidorum lib.IV.35. Alexander quidam Philosophus ἀσκητὴς vocatur.
units.tr: They arose from the Jews; from the Sadducees came the Gnostics; from the Essenes, the ascetics [ἀσκηταὶ] of the Jews, whose life, our Essenes, Philo describes. The name Asketai was given by the ancients to those who pursued a rather strict way of life, a term taken over from the philosophers, who used the word asceticism [ἀσκήσεως] for the exercise of virtue and abstinence. So in Arrian, Dissertations book 3, there is a chapter headed on asceticism [περὶ ἀσκήσεως]; and in Artemidorus, book 4, chapter 35, a certain philosopher Alexander is called an ascetic [ἀσκητής].

units.la: XXXVII.
units.tr: XXXVII.

units.la: Sed conspicui magis Gnosimachorum Patriarchæ Pharisæi fuerunt. Hi enim ex חסידים, ὅσιοις, Sanctis, Asidæis dictis, nec non צדיקים justis illis, quos ante captivitatem Babylonicam eximium nomen habuisse, ex 1.Macchab.II.42.VII.13. 2.Macch. XIV 6. colligitur, & ab incunabilis suis non sectam, sed συνάγμα ὅσιον, devotiorum Judæorum compagem fuisse constat; oriundi sunt, multum degeneres licet, quia pro vera sanctitate simulatam & fucatam coluerunt, sectamque fecerunt. Quandiu enim superrorogatio & præcifitas usu duntaxat recepta fuit, sectæ loco in populo Dei non fuit. Ast ubi supererrogationis præcepta in canones redacta sunt, & ἐκκαθασμὸς in legem abiit, tum verò ex חסידים prodierunt δογματισταὶ, qui se פרושים Pharisæos, hoc est, rum ab Asidæis ipsis κεχωρισμένες separatos dixerunt, & quæ prisci sponte sua secerunt, eorum faciendorum severam legem hi sibi dixerunt. Quam in rem plura Scaliger in Elencho Triharefii Nic.Serrarii,cap.22. dixit.
units.tr: But the Pharisees were the more conspicuous patriarchs of the opponents of the Gnostics. For they were named from the Hasidim [חסידים], the holy ones [ὅσιοι], Saints, Asideans, and also from those righteous ones [צדיקים] who, as is gathered from 1 Macc. 2.42, 7.13, and 2 Macc. 14.6, enjoyed an outstanding name before the Babylonian captivity. From their beginnings it is clear that they were not a sect but a holy association, a fellowship of the more devoted Jews; they are descended from these, though they became much degenerate, because instead of true holiness they cultivated a feigned and painted sanctity, and so made a sect. For as long as works of supererogation and extra strictness were received only in practice, there was no sect among the people of God. But when the precepts of supererogation were reduced to canons, and the exceptional strictness passed into law, then indeed from the Hasidim arose the dogmatists [δογματισταὶ], who called themselves Pharisees [פרושים], that is, those separated from the Asideans themselves [κεχωρισμένες]. What the early ones had done of their own accord, they made a severe law of doing. Scaliger has said more on this in his Refutation of the Trihaeresium of Nicolaus Serarius, chapter 22.

units.la: XXXVIII.
units.tr: XXXVIII.

units.la: Ex historia Evangelii, & aliunde etiam constat, qualis hominum istorum sanctitas fuerit. Forum enim vox talis vulgi aures feriit: קרוב אליך אל תגש בי כי קדשתיך Accede ad te (facesse à me) ne tangas me, quia sanctior te sum, Esaj.LXV.5. q.d. Ἐκὰς, ἐκὰς βέβηλοι. Procul, procul profani. Discernebant nempe se Curii hi simulati à populo tum vitæ munditia, per abstinentiam à cibis pollutis: tum sanctimonia externa, quam incessu, venæ sectione, & capite & dorso terram versus sponte inclinato & detorto, repræsentarunt. Alia etiam non pauca Christus iis exprobravit. velut quòd non ederent, nisi in lavandis manibus πυγμῇ νίψωνται, usque ad pugnum, ob aquæ per totam illam brachii partem, quæ πυγμὴ dicitur, defluxum; adeóque à digitorum radice seu propagine ad cubitum usque, lavarentur, Marc VII.3. quòd à foro reduces anxiè admodum se purgarent, & calices, sextarios, & lectos lavarent, ib. v.4. quòd phylacteria sua dilatarent, Matth.XXIII.5. omnem in lotionibus, cibis, vestibus sanctitatem ita reponentes; aliáque similia, in quorum minutiis ingens hypocrisis latebat, quia à doctoribus... ctoribus velut sedentibus in cathedra Mosis authoritatem consecuta sunt, & ceu pietatis seriæ opera, rigidè exigi sueverunt. qua in re inprimis Pharisaicum fermentum constitit. Præcipuum illud erat, quòd minutiis talibus inhærentes, τὰ βαρύτερα τῆς νόμε, τὴν κρίσιν, καὶ τὸν ἔλεον, καὶ τὴν πίστιν graviora legis, judicium, misericordiam & fidem neglexerunt, Matth.XXIII.23. sanctimoniam singularem præ se tulerunt, qui intus odio, invidia, rapacitate corrupti, histrioniam in mundo agebant, & externis operibus & oculiferiis Deo hominibusque se imponere posse sperabant. Quia enim gloriam hominum magis quàm gloriam Dei dilexerunt, Joh.XII.43. iccirco oculis omnia dederunt, ut ab hominibus spectarentur; & in ceremoniis externis, auctioribus etiam, obeundis, pietatis cardinem reposuerunt. Atque ita facile eò prolapsi sunt, ut legem sibi præstitu non impossibilem imaginati, ex illa etiam, imò externa tantùm ejus disciplina & cortice, justitiam propriam stabilire præsumerent. Quod iis non aliter, quàm conscientiæ propriæ de peccato convictæ fraudem faciendo, legem viribus hominum accommodando, ex peccato non peccatum faciendo, & tantum de legis perfectione demendo, quantum impersectionis sibi conscii fuerunt, facere licuit.
units.tr: It is clear from the history of the Gospel, and from elsewhere too, what sort of holiness these men had. For the voice of such people struck the ears of the crowd: "Keep off, do not touch me, for I am holier than you" [קרוב אליך אל תגש בי כי קדשתיך], Isa. 65.5, that is, Away, away, profane ones! Far off, far off! [ἐκὰς, ἐκὰς βέβηλοι]. These pretended guardians of the Law distinguished themselves from the people, both by the cleanness of their life, through abstinence from unclean foods, and by external holiness, which they displayed in their gait, in bloodletting, and in bowing and twisting head and back voluntarily toward the ground. Christ also rebuked them for many other things: for example, that they did not eat unless they washed their hands [πυγμῇ νίψωνται], up to the fist, because of the flow of water over that whole part of the arm called the fist, so that they washed from the root of the fingers up to the elbow, Mark 7.3; that when they came back from the marketplace they purified themselves very anxiously, and washed cups, pitchers and couches, ibid. v. 4; that they enlarged their phylacteries, Matt. 23.5, placing all holiness in washings, foods and clothing; and other similar things, in the smallest details of which lay hidden a great hypocrisy. For these things had gained authority from the teachers who sat, as it were, in the seat of Moses, and they were accustomed to exact them rigidly as works of serious piety. In this matter especially the Pharisaic leaven consisted. The chief fault was this: clinging to such trifles, they neglected the weightier matters of the law [τὰ βαρύτερα τῆς νόμου, τὴν κρίσιν, καὶ τὸν ἔλεον, καὶ τὴν πίστιν], judgment, mercy and faith, Matt. 23.23; they displayed a singular sanctimony, while inwardly corrupted by hatred, envy and rapacity, they played the hypocrite in the world, and hoped that by external works and eye-service they could deceive God and men. For because they loved the glory of men more than the glory of God, John 12.43, therefore they gave everything to the eyes, so that they might be watched by men; and in external ceremonies, even in the increased ones they performed, they placed the hinge of piety. And so they easily slipped into the state of imagining that the law was not impossible for them to fulfil, and presumed that from it, and indeed from its merely external discipline and bark, they could establish their own righteousness. This they could do only by defrauding their own conscience, which was convinced of sin, by adapting the law to human strength, by making what is sin not sin, and by subtracting from the perfection of the law as much as they were aware of their own imperfection.

units.la: XXXIX.
units.tr: XXXIX.

units.la: Habet omnino Pharisaismus ἐλκυστικόν, quod homini, propriæ justitiæ typho inflato, & acri, veluti thyrso percussO, mirè arridet, eúmque adversus Deum & hominem elatum & ferocem reddit; quasi justitia sua utilitatem Deo afferat, & Deus omnibus, quæ homo ex se producit, delectetur. Homo etiam natura φιλαυτος, non φυλόθεος, seipsum & justitiam suam potiùs quàm Deum fortunæ suæ fabrum esse vult. Ideo Pharisaismus, & in universum Judaismus validissimas in Ecclesia Christiana sequiore & corrupta partes nactus est omnium illorum, qui ex operibus, & justitia legis, atque ἀσπίς sua, præterita fide in Christum, in qua notitia, & apprehensio ejusdem fiducialis est, justitiam & vitam sectantur; vel opera legis cum fide Evangelii commiscentes, utriusque perperam explicatæ obedientiam salutis causam faciunt. Ut meritò Apostolus pridem hortatus sit: Curantes, ne quis deficiens à gratia Dei, ne qua radix amaritudinis sursum germinans obturbet, & per hanc inquinentur multi, Hebr.XII.15. Magno enim in discrimine versantur, qui cum Pharisæis, Judæis & Justitiariis omnibus in vita puritatem quærunt, neglecta vera sanctificatione, sine qua neminem visurum Deum, Apostolus v.14. dixerat; quæ non in quavis justitia & sanctitate, sed in ἁγιασμῷ sanctificatione, hoc est, vera justitia ejusque fructu, libertate & charitate, ex fide minime simulata oriunda, 1. Timoth. 1: 5. consistunt. Eam qui negligunt, in eo statu sunt, ut sibi in justitia propria operum externorum apud homines splendentium exercitio, atque omissione quorundam peccatorum vituperabilium, & obedientia rituum mire placeant, atque inde vitam & salutem expectent, unde mortis & damnationis æternæ incrementum sequitur. A Christo prorsus sejuncti estis, quotquot in lege justificamini; gratia excidistis, Gal. V. 4. Quæ illa radix amaritudinis, sursum geminans, & cuncta obturbans, Heb. XII. 15. nec non שרש פרה ולענה radix fructificans veneno & absinthio, Deut. XXX. 18. 19. est. uti Judaizantium, Catharorum, Pelagianorum, Novatianorum, Donatistarum, Antichristi inprimis, ex operibus propriis, sepulta vera cognitione Christi, veráque justitia, salutem sibi spondentium, historia demonstrat.
units.tr: Pharisaism certainly has an attractive power [ἐλκυστικόν]. It delights a man whose pride in his own righteousness has been puffed up, and who has been struck, as with a sharp thyrsus, and it makes him proud and fierce against God and man, as though his righteousness brought some advantage to God, and God took pleasure in everything that man produces from himself. Man is also by nature self-loving [φίλαυτος] rather than God-loving [φύλοθεος]: he wants to be the maker of his own fortune, and of himself and his own righteousness rather than of God's. Therefore Pharisaism, and Judaism in general, has gained very strong footing in the later and corrupted part of the Christian Church, among all those who pursue justice and life from works, from the righteousness of the law, and from their own shield [ἀσπίς], neglecting faith in Christ, in which the knowledge and trusting apprehension of him consists; or who mix the works of the law with the faith of the Gospel and, misunderstanding both, make their obedience the cause of salvation.
